course.title: AI Agents and Agent Architecture
course.description: Design agents you can trust: the loop, tools and protocols, memory, patterns for planning and composition, and the controls for permissions, injection, traces, evaluation and oversight.
course.audience: A developer who has called a language model from code. ai-engineering (tokens, prompts, retrieval, evaluation) is the recommended earlier course. Coding assistants are covered separately in ai-assisted-engineering.

paragraphs: An agent is a program in which a language model chooses its own next step, calls tools and reads what comes back, and building one raises problems that a single model call does not. The number of steps a run takes, what the run costs, what the agent is allowed to touch, what happens when a hostile sentence reaches it and how anyone can tell that it works all have to be decided before it is trusted with real work. This course takes those problems in the order a developer meets them.

It begins with the loop at the core of an agent and with the choice between a workflow, a copilot and an agent, and then takes up the tools an agent calls, the protocols that connect them, and what the agent keeps in its context as a run grows. The middle lessons compare the patterns for planning, for composing model calls and for dividing work among several agents, with the arithmetic of what each one costs. The last lessons turn to governing agents: permissions enforced on the server, prompt injection and the lethal trifecta, traces and measures, evaluation by repeated trials, and the staged rollout of autonomy.

Most lessons ask you to work something out, such as the cost of a run, the time of parallel branches, the chance that a vote is right or the reliability of ten steps in a row, and a calculator is allowed where the arithmetic is incidental. The course assumes that you have called a language model from code and know what tokens and prompts are, which AI Engineering covers, and it leaves coding assistants to a course of their own.
outcomes: You'll be able to choose between a workflow, a copilot and an agent for a task.
You'll be able to trace an agent loop and compute its cost and reliability.
You'll be able to design tools and a server-side permission model.
You'll be able to recognise prompt injection and break the lethal trifecta.
You'll be able to instrument and evaluate an agent and stage its rollout.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Python for Data Analysis, How Computers Solve Problems, Probability and Statistics, AI Engineering: LLMs, Prompting, Retrieval and Evaluation.

modules.title: Anatomy of an agent
modules.description: What separates an agent from a workflow, the loop at its core, its tools and protocol, and what it remembers.

modules.title: Architecture patterns
modules.description: Planning, composed workflows and multiple agents, and the costs each pattern carries.

modules.title: Governing agents
modules.description: Permissions, injection, traces, evaluation and human oversight: the controls that decide whether an agent can be trusted with a task.

concepts.title: Workflow
concepts.summary: Model calls and tools orchestrated by code along predefined paths.

concepts.title: Agent
concepts.summary: A system in which the model decides its own next steps and tool use within a loop.

concepts.title: Autonomy ladder
concepts.summary: Script, model-assisted workflow, copilot, agent: more freedom, less predictability.

concepts.title: Agent loop
concepts.summary: Repeat: model sees context, picks an action, the result is appended, until a stop condition holds.

concepts.title: Step budget
concepts.summary: A hard limit on iterations, tokens or time.

concepts.title: Compounding error
concepts.summary: Per-step reliability multiplies across steps.

concepts.title: Tool description
concepts.summary: The name, purpose, parameters and limits that the model reads when choosing a tool.

concepts.title: Read versus write tool
concepts.summary: A read tool only fetches; a write tool changes state.

concepts.title: Idempotency key
concepts.summary: A caller-supplied token so a repeated request has the effect of one.

concepts.title: Model Context Protocol
concepts.summary: An open protocol by which a client application discovers and calls tools, resources and prompts on a server.

concepts.title: JSON-RPC
concepts.summary: A message format of method, parameters and id, with a matching result or error.

concepts.title: Transport
concepts.summary: The channel carrying messages: standard input/output for local servers, HTTP for remote ones.

concepts.title: Working context
concepts.summary: What is in the prompt on this step.

concepts.title: Compaction
concepts.summary: Summarising old turns to free room.

concepts.title: External memory
concepts.summary: Notes and files the agent writes and reads back by tool.

concepts.title: Reason-act loop
concepts.summary: Interleave a short reasoning step with an action and an observation.

concepts.title: Plan then execute
concepts.summary: Write the whole plan first, then carry out steps, replanning on failure.

concepts.title: Reflection
concepts.summary: Critique the result or failure and retry with the critique.

concepts.title: Prompt chaining
concepts.summary: A fixed sequence of model calls, each taking the previous output.

concepts.title: Parallelisation
concepts.summary: Independent subtasks run at once (sectioning) or the same task run several times (voting).

concepts.title: Evaluator-optimiser
concepts.summary: One call proposes, another critiques, and the loop repeats until accepted.

concepts.title: Handoff
concepts.summary: One agent passing control and context to another.

concepts.title: Context isolation
concepts.summary: Giving a subagent only the context its task needs.

concepts.title: Agent contract
concepts.summary: The defined inputs, outputs and permissions between two agents.

concepts.title: Least privilege
concepts.summary: Giving an agent only the access its task needs.

concepts.title: Approval gate
concepts.summary: A human decision required before a risky action runs.

concepts.title: Audit log
concepts.summary: An append-only record of each action with who, what and why.

concepts.title: Lethal trifecta
concepts.summary: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to communicate externally, in one agent.

concepts.title: Untrusted content
concepts.summary: Any text the agent reads that an attacker could have written.

concepts.title: Privilege separation
concepts.summary: Splitting work so that the part reading untrusted content has no powerful tools.

concepts.title: Trace
concepts.summary: The record of one run as nested spans for model calls, retrievals and tool calls.

concepts.title: 95th percentile
concepts.summary: The value below which 95% of observations fall (nearest rank: the ceil(0.95·n)th smallest).

concepts.title: Cost per success
concepts.summary: Total spend divided by the number of successful tasks.

concepts.title: Trajectory
concepts.summary: The sequence of actions an agent took, not only its final answer.

concepts.title: pass@k
concepts.summary: The chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds.

concepts.title: pass^k
concepts.summary: The chance that all k attempts succeed.

concepts.title: Oversight point
concepts.summary: Where a person approves, samples or can stop the agent.

concepts.title: Staged rollout
concepts.summary: Shadow, assist, then act, each gated by evidence.

concepts.title: Autonomy decision record
concepts.summary: A written decision stating the autonomy level, why, and the trigger for changing it.

lessons.title: Workflow, copilot or agent

steps.headline: A workflow is built so that code chooses each step, and an agent is built so that the model does.

lead.text: Return to the refund request. Suppose the system always classifies the message, looks up the order, checks the policy and writes a reply, in that order, with a language model doing the classifying, the policy check and the writing. The model is called three times, yet it never decides what happens next, because the order was fixed in code before the request arrived. In its guide to building effective agents, Anthropic's engineering team calls a system of this kind a **workflow**: language models and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths.

Now suppose the same system is given only the customer's message and a set of tools it may call. The model chooses a tool, receives the result, chooses again, and stops when it judges that the request has been dealt with. The guide calls this an **agent**: a system in which the model directs its own process and its use of tools, within a loop. The definition sits close to the one in Russell and Norvig's *Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach*, where an agent is anything that perceives its environment and acts on it, with the added condition that here the model is the part that chooses the action.

The difference therefore comes down to one question, **who decides the next step**. The number of model calls does not settle it, since a workflow may call a model ten times and an agent only once, and the presence of tools does not settle it either, since a workflow may call a tool at every step.

A support system runs three model calls in an order fixed by its code: it classifies the message, then retrieves the matching policy text, then writes the answer. Apply the question from the last screen to this design.

reveal.text: The code fixed the order before the request arrived, so the design is a workflow however many model calls it makes. A fourth call added to the pipeline would not change that.

steps.headline: Between a script and an agent there are two more rungs, and each moves another decision from code to the model.

lead.text: The workflow and the agent are the two ends of a scale, and it helps to name the rungs between them. At the bottom is the **script**, ordinary code in which no model chooses anything. Above it is the workflow, in which code still fixes the order but a model does work inside some of the steps, as in the refund pipeline. Next comes the **copilot**, in which the model proposes the next step and a person approves, edits or rejects it before anything happens. At the top is the agent, in which the model chooses the step and the tool with no person in between, until it decides that the work is done. Together the four rungs form the **autonomy ladder**.

afterFigure.text: Moving up a rung hands one more decision to the model, which is where the flexibility comes from: a model can handle a request that nobody wrote a branch for. The same move removes something, because code can be tested on every input it will see and a model's choices cannot, so each rung up is *less predictable* than the one below it. The buttons in the figure show where the decision sits on each rung.

diagram.alt: A line of four rungs from script to agent. Each case highlights one rung and says who decides the next step: code for a script, code for the order in a workflow, a person approving the model in a copilot, and the model in an agent.
diagram.caption: The decision moves from code to the model as you climb. Use the buttons to move between rungs.

lead.text: Suppose the refund workflow makes 3 model calls per request, at $0.01 a call. An agent built for the same task makes more calls, because each tool result is followed by another model call, and over many requests it averages 12 calls at the same price. Before the next screen explains why, work out how much more the agent costs.

reveal.text: The agent costs $0.12 per request against $0.03, which is four times as much. The ratio equals the ratio of calls because the price per call is the same.

steps.headline: Each rung up buys flexibility and costs predictability, money, speed and the ease of explaining what happened.

lead.text: The agent in the last question cost four times as much, and cost is one of several things that change as you climb. An agent's calls are chosen as it goes, so its **latency**, the time a customer waits for the reply, grows with the number of calls and varies from one request to the next, whereas a workflow takes almost the same time on every request. Correctness moves in both directions: an agent can handle requests that the workflow's branches never anticipated, and it can also wander into the wrong tool, which a fixed path cannot do. Auditability, the ability to say afterwards why something happened, is highest for a script, where the code is the explanation, and lowest for an agent, where the explanation is a record of what the model chose. The impact of a failure depends on what the system is allowed to do, since an agent that can issue refunds can issue a wrong one.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets the four rungs against two needs. When the refund policy is fixed and the only hard part is reading free text, a workflow meets the need, and the agent meets it too but at four times the cost. When every dispute needs a different investigation and there are too many for a person to handle, only the agent meets the need. The rule that follows is to choose **the lowest rung that meets the need**, and to say in advance what evidence would justify climbing.

steps.headline: Choose the rung for the standard refund process, then price it for a month.

workedSteps.text: List the steps the process needs: classify the message, look up the order, check the 30-day refund policy, and write the reply.
Ask whether the order of the steps ever depends on what an earlier step returns. Here it does not, because every request needs the same four steps in the same order.
A fixed order means code can hold the path, so the lowest rung that meets the need is a workflow. The lookup is plain code, and the other three steps are model calls.
Price one request at $0.01 for each model call.
Multiply by the 1,000 requests in a month to find what the workflow costs for the month, in dollars.

steps.headline: Choose the rung for disputed refunds, where each case needs a different investigation.

workedSteps.text: Disputed cases vary: one needs the courier's tracking, another the customer's earlier orders, another a second photograph. The steps cannot be listed before the case has been read.
A script and a workflow both need the path in code, so neither meets the need. A copilot would meet it, but only with a person on each of 400 cases a day, and the team has no one to spare.
That leaves the top rung. Name it.

lead.text: A team proposes an agent to answer the question "Where is my order?". Every such answer comes from one order lookup followed by one templated sentence, and no request has ever needed anything else.

reveal.text: Where the steps never vary there is nothing for a model to decide, so the cheapest design that meets the need is also the most predictable one.

steps.headline: Starting on a low rung can be undone, so a design should say what would make it climb.

lead.text: Starting low does not commit a team to staying there. A design that records its rung should also record a **trigger**, a measurable condition under which the next rung becomes worth its cost, such as the share of requests that the fixed path cannot resolve. Suppose the refund workflow resolves 94 requests in every 100 and the other 6 reach a person. Sending all 100 through an agent would multiply the cost of the 94 that the workflow already handles, whereas sending only the 6 to an agent pays the higher price on just the requests that need it.

A router that makes that split is itself a workflow, and it shows how the ladder is used in practice: different parts of one product can sit on different rungs, each at the lowest rung that meets its own need. The trigger turns the choice of a rung into a measurement, and it keeps the argument from being settled by how impressive an agent sounds.

A router sends 6% of the 2,000 refund requests a day straight to the agent, which costs $0.12 per request, and the rest through the workflow, which costs $0.03 per request. Ignore the router's own cost.

reveal.text: Most of the bill still comes from the workflow's 1,880 requests, but the agent's 120 requests add up to about a fifth of the total, so the trigger that sends requests to the agent also controls the budget.

lessons.orientation: Place a refund process on the autonomy ladder and choose the lowest rung that meets the need.
lessons.nextAction: Follow the agent loop step by step and see what stops it and how errors compound.

blocks.text: A customer writes that an order arrived damaged and asks for the money back. To deal with it, a support system has to decide what kind of message this is, find the order, check the refund policy and send a reply, and there is more than one way to build that. In one design, ordinary code runs the four steps in a fixed order and calls a language model to classify the message, check the policy and write the reply. In another, the model is given tools such as an order lookup and a refund button, and left to decide which to use and when to stop.

Both designs answer the customer, but they differ in who decides what happens next, and that difference changes what the system costs, how long the customer waits and how easily anyone can explain afterwards what it did. The figure draws the two designs for this one request: the steps are much the same, but in the first the code draws the arrows in advance and in the second the model draws them as it goes.

diagram.alt: The same refund request handled two ways. In the first, code runs classify, look up order, check policy and write reply in a fixed order. In the second, a model repeatedly chooses among four tools.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a process on the ladder from script to agent, compare the cost of two designs, and choose the lowest rung that meets the need.
intro.whyItMatters: Autonomy is bought with cost, delay and predictability, so a design should not pay for more than the task needs.

recap.keyIdea: The autonomy ladder runs from script to workflow to copilot to agent, and the lowest rung that meets the need is the right one, because each rung up costs predictability, money and time.

blocks.text: A workflow lets code fix the path and an agent lets the model choose it, so the test is who decides the next step, whatever the number of model calls. Each rung up the ladder hands the model more of the decisions, and the gap between a three-call workflow and a twelve-call agent, four to one in cost, shows the price of that freedom. A design should therefore start at the lowest rung that meets the need and name the measurement that would justify climbing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows the agent rung in detail, tracing its loop step by step and showing what stops it.

lessons.title: The agent loop

steps.headline: An agent runs one loop: the model sees the context, chooses an action, and the result is added to the context.

lead.text: At each step of an agent's run, the model is given the **context**, which holds the goal and everything that has happened since, and it replies with an action: usually a call to one of its tools. The code around the model carries out that call and appends the result, called the **observation**, to the context, and the model is then called again with the longer context. This cycle is the **agent loop**, and it is the whole mechanism, since everything an agent appears to do is some number of passes through it.

The figure follows one run for the refund goal from the last lesson. In step 1 the model chooses to look up the order, and the result joins the context. In step 2 it chooses to check the policy with the facts it has just been given. In step 3 it replies with a sentence and no tool call, and that absence is what ends the run. The pattern is the one that Yao and colleagues described in the ReAct paper, in which a model alternates between reasoning and acting and reads each result before choosing the next step, and it is also how Anthropic describes agents: language models using tools, based on feedback from their environment, in a loop.

diagram.alt: Three stages of one agent run. The context starts with a goal about order 4471. After step 1 it holds a lookup call and its result, after step 2 a policy check and its result, and after step 3 the final answer, which has no tool call and ends the run.

lead.text: The run in the figure ended at step 3 with a final answer and no tool call. Think about what the code around the model did at each step before you answer.

reveal.text: The model was called once per pass, and the third pass produced the answer, so the loop made three model calls and two tool calls. The final answer is the model's output of a pass like any other.

lead.text: A tool returns an error every time the model calls it, and the model keeps choosing the same tool in the hope that the next attempt will work. It never decides that it is finished, and nothing in the code limits the run.

reveal.text: The model's own judgement that it is finished cannot be relied on, so the code needs a limit that does not depend on it. The next screen sets out the ways a loop can end.

steps.headline: A loop can end in four ways, and only a limit set in code is certain to happen.

lead.text: The loop in the last figure ended because the model wrote an answer, which is the way a well-behaved run finishes, but it is only one of four. A run can also end on an error that the code treats as fatal, for example a tool that has failed in the same way three times, or on a request from a person who watches the run and cancels it. The fourth is a **step budget**: a hard limit on the number of iterations, or on tokens or time, after which the code ends the loop whatever the model has chosen. Anthropic's guide to agents recommends stopping conditions of this kind, such as a maximum number of iterations, to keep control of a run.

The first three depend on something outside the code behaving as hoped: the model must decide that it is finished, the error must be recognised, a person must be watching. Only the budget is enforced by the loop itself. The program in the figure has no answer to wait for, and it still ends when the step reaches the budget of 4, because the condition `step < budget` is then false. An agent without such a limit runs until the model decides to stop, and a model that never decides to stop costs money on every pass.

diagram.code:
step = 0
budget = 4
while step < budget:
    step = step + 1

steps.headline: Every pass sends the whole context again, so the input a step costs grows with each step.

lead.text: The model keeps no memory between calls, which is why the code sends the context afresh each time, with the new call and result appended. The input to step 1 is the starting context, say 1,000 [[tokens|Chunks of text a model reads or writes. Met in AI Engineering.]], and each step then adds 400 tokens for the model's call and the tool's result. The input to step 2 is therefore 1,400 tokens, the input to step 3 is 1,800, and so on, rising by 400 each time. The model is billed for the whole input of every call, so the cost of a run is the *sum* of these inputs, not the size of the last one.

The trace in the figure adds up the inputs of the first four steps: 1,000 + 1,400 + 1,800 + 2,200, which comes to 6,400. A run twice as long costs more than twice as much, because each added step is more expensive than the one before it, and this is the first reason an agent's cost is harder to predict than a workflow's: the cost depends on how many steps the loop takes.

diagram.code:
tokens = 1000
total = 0
step = 1
while step <= 4:
    total = total + tokens
    tokens = tokens + 400
    step = step + 1

lead.text: Use the same pattern as the trace you have just followed: the input to step 1 is 1,000 tokens, and each later step adds 400. Add up the inputs for a run of six steps.

reveal.text: The six inputs are 1,000, 1,400, 1,800, 2,200, 2,600 and 3,000. The last step alone costs three times the first, which is why long runs are expensive.

lead.text: Suppose each step of an agent's run succeeds 90% of the time, and a step that fails spoils the run. The run needs three steps in a row, and the steps do not affect one another. Make a guess before the next screen explains how to work it out.

reveal.text: The three steps all have to succeed, so the chances multiply: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729. A run of three steps that are each 90% reliable succeeds only about 73% of the time.

steps.headline: Per-step reliability multiplies, so a long run of good steps can still be a poor bet.

lead.text: The arithmetic of the last question holds for any run. If each step succeeds with probability p, the steps are independent, and the task needs every one of n steps to succeed, then the chance of finishing is p multiplied by itself n times, written pⁿ. This is **compounding error**: a small chance of failure at each step, repeated, adds up to a large chance of failure over the run. It also means that the usual reading of a per-step figure is too generous, since a step that is right 95% of the time sounds dependable, and a ten-step task built from such steps is dependable only *about 60% of the time*.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the same 95% step in tasks of 5, 10 and 20 steps, which finish with probabilities of about 77%, 60% and 36%. The assumptions behind the numbers matter: real steps are not always independent, and a good agent can sometimes notice a failed step and retry it. Even so, the calculation gives the right instinct, that each step added to a run has a price in reliability, and that shortening a run can raise reliability more than improving each step slightly.

steps.headline: Find the chance that a 20-step run succeeds when each step succeeds 98% of the time.

workedSteps.text: All 20 steps must succeed, and the steps are independent, so the chance is 0.98 multiplied by itself 20 times.
A calculator takes the power in one operation. Enter 0.98 and raise it to the power 20.
Read the result and round it to two decimal places.

lead.text: A team improves its agent so that each step succeeds 99% of the time instead of 95%. The task is still ten steps long, and the steps are independent.

reveal.text: The run now finishes about 90% of the time, against about 60% before, so a four-point gain per step became a thirty-point gain over the run.

lead.text: A team sets a step budget of 8 for a run whose input is 1,000 tokens at step 1 and grows by 400 tokens at each later step. They want the most input the loop can ever read.

reveal.text: Because the budget caps the number of steps, it also caps the input, so the worst case is known before the run starts. The ceiling is a figure the team can price, which an unbounded loop cannot offer.

lessons.orientation: Trace an agent loop, set the limit that ends it, and work out what a run costs and how often it succeeds.
lessons.nextAction: Design the tools an agent calls, so that the loop has something useful to choose between.

blocks.text: A single call to a language model sends a prompt and receives text. An agent makes many calls, and each call carries the original request together with everything that has happened since, which is the model's earlier choices and the results they produced. If the starting context is 1,000 tokens and every step adds 400, the model reads 1,000 tokens at the first step, 1,400 at the second and 3,000 at the sixth, so the later steps cost far more than the early ones.

That growth is one reason an agent's behaviour has to be bounded, and compounding reliability is another: a step that works 95 times in 100 sounds dependable, but ten of them in a row do not. The figure shows the growth step by step, in tokens read at each step.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a run of the loop, add a stop condition and a step budget, and compute how cost and reliability change as a run lengthens.
intro.whyItMatters: Cost and reliability both depend on how many steps a run takes, and the code around the model has to bound that number.

recap.keyIdea: An agent loop repeats until a stop condition holds, and because each step re-reads a growing context and multiplies in a chance of failure, a step budget is what keeps cost and reliability in bounds.

blocks.text: The model sees the context, chooses an action, and the result is appended to the context before the model is called again, so the input grows by one call and one result at every step. A run ends when the model answers, when an error is fatal, when a person cancels it or when the step budget is reached, and only the last of these is certain to happen. Because per-step success rates multiply, a long run is much less reliable than any one of its steps, which makes a short run with a firm limit worth more than a long one that depends on the model deciding to stop.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes up the tools themselves: what a good tool description contains, and how a tool that changes things should be built.

lessons.title: Designing tools

steps.headline: The model chooses a tool from its description alone, so the description has to carry everything a careful reader would need.

lead.text: The model never sees a tool's code. What it receives is a **tool description**: the tool's name, a passage saying what it does, and a schema listing its parameters with their types. It chooses between tools by reading these, in just the way it reads a prompt, which makes a tool description part of the prompt and deserving of the same care. Anthropic's guide to building agents makes the same point about what it calls the agent-computer interface, saying that a team should put as much effort into the design of its tools as into the design of its prompts.

A description that does this work says what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each input means and in what form, and what comes back. The vague version in the figure leaves the model to guess at all of these, whereas the precise version tells it, for instance, that the order identifier comes from an earlier tool and that the amount may not exceed the order total. The *name* matters less than people expect, because two tools called `lookup` and `find` with the same thin description are indistinguishable to the model however well they are named.

diagram.alt: The same refund tool described two ways. The vague description says only that it refunds a customer. The precise one says what it does, when to use it and when not to, what each input means, and what it returns.
diagram.caption: The model reads these words to choose and call the tool. Use the buttons to compare the two descriptions.

lead.text: Here are three descriptions of one refund tool. Think about what a model that has never seen the tool, and cannot ask anyone about it, would need to be told.

reveal.text: The precise version names the situations in which to use the tool and the form of each input, which is exactly what the model cannot find out by trying. The overbroad one invites the model to refund whenever a customer is unhappy.

steps.headline: A read tool only fetches, a write tool changes something outside the conversation, and the difference decides how much care a tool needs.

lead.text: The five tools in the figure are easy to place once you ask what each leaves behind. `search_orders`, `get_customer` and `read_policy` only *fetch*: after any number of calls the shop is exactly as it was, which is why they are called **read tools**. `issue_refund` and `send_email` leave something behind, since money has left the shop and a message has reached a customer, and a tool of that kind is a **write tool**. Anything that creates, changes, deletes, sends or pays is a write tool, whatever its name suggests.

afterFigure.text: The distinction matters because the cost of a wrong call is so different. A wrong read costs a call and a little context, and the model can simply read again. A wrong write has consequences that cannot be taken back by calling another tool: an email cannot be unsent, and a refund that was not due has to be recovered by other means. For that reason the write tools are where a design spends its care, on tighter descriptions, narrower inputs and, as later lessons show, approval and permission checks. OWASP's 2025 list of risks for applications built on language models names *excessive agency*, giving a model tools that can do more than its task requires, as one of them.

diagram.alt: A table of the five support tools with columns for kind, what each touches, and whether it can be undone. The three read tools change nothing. The two write tools, issue_refund and send_email, move money or a message out of the shop and cannot be freely undone.
diagram.caption: Tools that only fetch change nothing; tools that act change the world. Use the buttons to see the tools sorted.

lead.text: The support team adds a tool, `cancel_subscription(customer_id)`, which ends a customer's plan from the next billing date. Use the test from the last screen: what does the tool leave behind?

reveal.text: Ending a plan changes what the customer is charged, and it cannot be seen as a fetch, so the tool is a write tool however gentle its name sounds.

steps.headline: A tool's error message is read by the model too, so it should name the problem and the next step.

lead.text: What a tool returns when it fails is read by the model in the same way as everything else in its context, and it decides what the model does next. An error that says only `400` leaves the model to guess, and a model that guesses often repeats the same call. An error that says `amount 5000 is more than the order total of 3800 cents; retry with an amount of at most 3800` gives the model the fact it lacked and the action to take, so the next step is likely to be the right one.

The better remedy is sometimes to make the mistake impossible. Anthropic's guide describes a coding agent whose tools took relative file paths, and which made errors with them once it had moved out of the root directory; the team changed the tool so that it required absolute paths, and the errors stopped. A tool whose inputs allow a mistake that the description can only warn against has a design fault that no wording will fully repair.

A write tool, `issue_refund(order_id, amount)`, pays out on every call. The agent calls it, the refund goes through, and the reply is lost in a network timeout. Hearing nothing, the agent calls it again, and then a third time, and both retries reach the server. Make a prediction before the next screen sets out the remedy.

reveal.text: Each call that reached the server paid out, so the customer has been refunded three times. The agent was right to retry, since it could not know that the first call had succeeded, and the fault lies in a tool that cannot tell a retry from a new request.

steps.headline: An idempotency key lets a server recognise a repeated request, so a write can be retried without being repeated.

lead.text: The agent in the last example cannot avoid retrying, because after a timeout it has no way to tell whether the request never arrived or its reply was lost. The remedy is to make the write safe to repeat. An operation is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, and a write is made idempotent with an **idempotency key**: a token chosen by the caller for one intended action and sent with every attempt at it. The server stores each key with the result of the first request that used it, and a later request with the same key receives that stored result without a second refund being made.

The key identifies the *action*, not the attempt. The caller makes one for each refund it intends and reuses it on every retry of that refund, so that three attempts at one refund make one refund; a different refund gets a different key. The figure shows the server in the two cases, and the second is the version that the tool in the lesson uses, `issue_refund(order_id, amount, idempotency_key)`.

diagram.alt: Two cases of an agent sending the same refund request three times after timeouts. Without an idempotency key the server makes three refunds. With the same key on every call the server makes one refund and returns the stored result to the later calls.
diagram.caption: The agent cannot know whether its first call arrived, so it retries. Use the buttons to compare the two servers.

steps.headline: Count how many refunds the server makes when five calls arrive with these keys, in this order: a, a, b, a, b.

workedSteps.text: The server starts with no keys stored. The first call carries key a, which it has not seen, so it makes a refund and stores a with the result.
The second call also carries a. The key is stored, so the server returns the stored result and makes no refund.
The third call carries b, a new key, so it makes a second refund and stores b.
The fourth call repeats a and the fifth repeats b. Both keys are stored, so neither makes a refund.
Count the refunds the server made over the five calls.

lead.text: A team builds the key for each refund from the order number alone, so that every call about order 4471 carries the key `refund-4471`. A customer is owed two partial refunds on that order, $10 and then $15, and the agent makes the two calls on different days.

reveal.text: The server found a stored key on the second call and returned the first refund's result, so the customer received $10 and never the $15. A key must identify the intended action, which here means the refund, and an order can have more than one.

lessons.orientation: Classify tools as read or write, write a description the model can use, and make a write tool safe to retry.
lessons.nextAction: Meet the protocol that lets one agent use tools from many servers.

blocks.text: A support agent has five tools: it can search orders, fetch a customer record, read the refund policy, issue a refund and send an email. The model never sees the code behind any of them. For each tool it receives a name, a description and a list of typed parameters, and everything it does with the tool follows from reading those few lines.

That makes the description the place where most mistakes either start or are prevented, and it raises a second problem for the tools that change things outside the conversation, which is what to do when the agent calls one and never hears back. The figure shows the tools and then one definition as the model receives it.

diagram.alt: Two views of a support agent's tools. The first lists five tool names with one-line descriptions: search_orders, get_customer, read_policy, issue_refund and send_email. The second shows one tool as the model receives it, with a name, a description and typed parameters, and no code.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a tool as read or write, judge whether a description is usable, and explain how an idempotency key makes a retried write safe.
intro.whyItMatters: Tools are the only way an agent acts, so their descriptions and their behaviour on retry decide whether a run is safe.

recap.keyIdea: A tool is the model's only view of an action, so its description has to be precise, its writes have to be told apart from its reads, and every write has to be safe to retry.

blocks.text: The model chooses and calls tools by reading their descriptions and their error messages, which are therefore part of the prompt and need the same care. A read tool changes nothing and can be called again at will, whereas a write tool leaves an effect that cannot be taken back. Because a reply can be lost after a write has succeeded, a write is given an idempotency key chosen for one intended action, so that three attempts at the action make one change.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the protocol that lets an agent discover and call tools offered by other programs, and at how agents talk to each other.

lessons.title: Tool protocols: MCP and agent-to-agent

steps.headline: A shared protocol turns the work of connecting every application to every tool into the work of connecting each to the protocol once.

lead.text: Every tool that an agent can use has to be connected to the application that runs the agent, and without an agreed way of doing it each application needs its own code for each tool. If there are N applications and M tools, that is N × M integrations, and each new tool or application adds a whole row or column to the work. The **Model Context Protocol**, or **MCP**, which Anthropic introduced in November 2024 as an open specification, replaces those integrations with one agreed message format: an application implements the client side once, a tool provider implements the server side once, and any client can then use any server, so the work comes to N + M implementations.

MCP is therefore a wire protocol, a specification of the messages that two programs exchange, and it is not a framework for building agents. It says nothing about how an agent plans or how its loop is written; it says how an application finds out which tools a server offers and how it asks the server to run one.
Four applications each need to use six tools, and no protocol is shared, so every application is wired to every tool separately. Use the idea from the last screen to count the work.

reveal.text: With a shared protocol the same four applications and six tools need only 4 + 6 = 10 implementations, which is why the gap widens as either number grows.

steps.headline: MCP has three roles: the host owns the model, the client holds one connection, and the server describes and runs the tools.

lead.text: The protocol names three parts. The **host** is the application the user is working in, and it contains the model. Inside the host, a **client** holds a connection to one server and speaks the protocol on the host's behalf. The **server** is the program that offers tools, and it does two things: it describes the tools it has, and it runs one when asked. The figure shows the three, joined by JSON-RPC messages, a format that the next screens take apart.

The second view of the figure shows who decides what, which is where a common misunderstanding arises. The model, which is in the host, reads the tool descriptions and chooses a tool; the client sends the call; and the server runs the tool and returns what it produced. A server does not choose which of its tools the model uses, any more than a shop chooses what a customer buys. It tells the host what exists and carries out what it is told.

diagram.alt: A host application on the left holding a model and a client, and a server on the right with three tools, joined by JSON-RPC messages. The second view marks who does what: the model chooses a tool, the client sends the call, and the server runs the tool.
diagram.caption: The host owns the model and the choice; the server describes tools and runs them. Use the buttons to switch views.

lead.text: The model has decided to call `search_orders`, and the client has sent the call over the connection. Think about which of the three roles holds the code that looks up the orders.

reveal.text: The server runs the tool, and the host only receives its result. This split is what lets a tool be written once and used by any application that speaks the protocol.

steps.headline: A JSON-RPC message names an operation in its method, carries its inputs in params, and pairs request and reply through the id.

lead.text: MCP's messages are written in **JSON-RPC** 2.0, a small standard for calling a named operation on another program. A request has four members. The `jsonrpc` member gives the version, `method` names the operation, `params` holds its inputs, and `id` is a number or string chosen by the sender. The reply carries the same `id`, which is how the sender knows which request it answers, and it holds either a `result` or an `error`, never both.

afterFigure.text: The request in the figure asks for the operation `tools/call`, and its `params` say which tool to run, `search_orders`, and with what arguments, a customer identifier. The response repeats `id` 7 and carries the tool's output as text. A tool that ran and failed also returns a result, with `isError` set to true, so that the model can read the error message, whereas a request the server cannot understand at all comes back as a JSON-RPC `error`. A message with no `id` is a notification, to which no reply is made.

diagram.alt: A JSON-RPC request and its response. The request carries jsonrpc 2.0, id 7, the method tools/call and params naming the tool search_orders with the argument customer c-42. The response carries the same id 7 and a result holding the tool's text.

lead.text: Here is a request from the same session: {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/list"}. Read its members against the figure.

reveal.text: The `method` member holds the operation, here `tools/list`, which asks the server for the tools it offers. The `id` of 3 will come back on the reply.

steps.headline: A session begins with an initialise exchange, after which the client lists the tools and then calls them.

lead.text: A connection starts with a short exchange in which each side states what it can do. The client sends an `initialize` request giving the protocol version it supports and its capabilities, and the server answers with its own version and capabilities, which include whether it offers tools. The client then sends a notification that it is ready. Only after this exchange does the client send `tools/list`, whose result is the list of tools, each with a name, a description and a schema for its inputs, and these are exactly the descriptions the model reads when it chooses.

The third phase is the one the agent loop uses, and it repeats: each time the model chooses a tool, the client sends a `tools/call` and waits for the result, which joins the context. The figure shows the order of the messages, with the current phase marked in blue and the later ones dashed.

diagram.alt: A sequence diagram of an MCP session between a client and a server. The client sends initialize and the server answers, the client sends an initialized notification, then asks tools/list and receives the list, and finally sends tools/call and receives the result. Each view highlights one phase.
diagram.caption: Messages flow between client and server in a fixed order. Use the buttons to move through the three phases.

lead.text: A tool server runs on the same machine as the host, and the host starts it as a program of its own. The messages have to travel between the two programs in some way. Before the next screen, name the simplest channel the two could use.

reveal.text: MCP defines two transports, the channels that carry its messages. For a local server the host starts the program and exchanges messages over its **standard input and output**, known as stdio. A remote server is reached over HTTP, in the form the specification calls Streamable HTTP, so that one server can serve many clients on other machines.

steps.headline: Match the reply to the request, then read what it says.

workedSteps.text: The client sent a `tools/call` request with `id` 7 for the tool `search_orders` with the customer c-42.
A reply arrives. JSON-RPC pairs a reply with its request by the `id` alone, so the reply must carry the same id as the request it answers.
State the id that the reply must carry.
Inside `result`, the `content` holds the text `orders 4471, 4502`, and `isError` is false, so the tool ran and found two orders.

lead.text: A company has 6 applications and 9 tool servers. Count the work done by a protocol: compare the number of bespoke integrations with the number of implementations of the shared protocol, and find the difference.

reveal.text: The shared protocol needs 6 + 9 = 15 implementations against 6 × 9 = 54 bespoke integrations. Each new tool server then costs one implementation, where before it cost six.

steps.headline: MCP connects an agent to tools, and a separate protocol, A2A, connects an agent to other agents.

lead.text: MCP is built for the case where the other side is a *tool server*: it lists tools, runs them and returns results, and it has no goals of its own. Agents also need to work with other agents, often ones built by other organisations, and that is a different problem, since the other party plans and decides for itself and a job may take a long time. The Agent2Agent protocol, written A2A, is designed for it: an agent publishes a description of what it can do, often called an agent card, and another agent can discover it, send it a task and follow the task's status until a result comes back.

The two protocols are complementary and one product can use both: an agent may use MCP for its own tools and A2A to hand a task to another agent. Confusing them leads to design mistakes, such as treating a tool server as if it could negotiate, or an agent as if it were a function to be called.

diagram.alt: Two protocols compared. In MCP an agent host connects to tool servers such as order tools, email tools and policy files. In A2A one agent, a shop agent, sends a task to another agent, a courier agent run by another company, and receives its status and result.
diagram.caption: MCP connects an agent to tools and data; A2A connects an agent to another agent. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The courier's agent plans and decides for itself, so handing it a task is the case A2A was designed for. The order database is a tool, which MCP serves.

blocks.text: Suppose three applications each need to use five tools. If every application is wired directly to every tool, someone writes and maintains 15 separate integrations, and the sixth tool or the fourth application adds another five or three. The work grows as a product, and it is repeated by every team that builds an agent.

A shared protocol changes the arithmetic, since each application and each tool then has to speak the protocol once, which makes 3 + 5 = 8 pieces of work. The Model Context Protocol is such a protocol for agents and tools, and this lesson reads one of its messages line by line. The figure shows the two wirings side by side.

diagram.alt: Two wirings of three applications and five tools. Without a protocol every application is connected directly to every tool, 15 connections. With a shared protocol each application and each tool connects only to the protocol, 8 connections.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a JSON-RPC tool request, say which side owns each part of MCP, and tell MCP apart from an agent-to-agent protocol.
intro.whyItMatters: Most real agents reach their tools through a protocol, so reading its messages is how you tell what an agent can do and what it did.

recap.keyIdea: MCP is a wire protocol in which a host's client discovers and calls the tools of a server through JSON-RPC messages, and the model, not the server, chooses which tool to call.

blocks.text: A host contains the model, a client holds one connection to one server, and the server describes its tools and runs them. A request names its operation in `method`, carries inputs in `params` and is answered by a reply with the same `id`, and a session runs through initialisation, `tools/list` and then `tools/call`, over stdio for a local server or HTTP for a remote one. A2A is a different protocol, for an agent that hands work to another agent, so the two are used together and not instead of one another.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to what an agent keeps in its context as a run grows, and what it does when the context fills.

lessons.title: Memory and context management

steps.headline: The context window is a budget that every step draws on, and a larger window does not remove the need to plan it.

lead.text: At each step the model reads a context that holds its instructions, the descriptions of its tools, the conversation so far and every tool result that has come back. These together are the **working context**, which is what is in the prompt on this step, and the **context window** is the most that a model can read in a single call. The figure takes a window of 100,000 tokens, and the first view shows 62,000 of them in use: 8,000 for instructions and tool descriptions, 30,000 for the conversation and 24,000 for tool results. The second view adds a tool result of 21,000 tokens, which brings the total to 83,000 and past the dashed line at 80,000, the point at which this agent has been set to compact its context.

afterFigure.text: A larger window does not make the budget unnecessary, for two reasons. Every token in the context is read again at every step and paid for each time, as the cost arithmetic of the [[agent loop|The cycle in which the model chooses an action and the result is added to the context. Met in 'The agent loop'.]] showed, so a long context makes every later step dearer. And a model may use information in a very long context less reliably than information in a short one, so a context that holds everything is not guaranteed to be one that the model uses well.

diagram.alt: A bar for a 100,000-token context window. In the first view 62,000 tokens are in use: 8,000 instructions, 30,000 conversation and 24,000 tool results, below a dashed compaction line at 80,000. In the second a 21,000-token tool result brings the total to 83,000, past the line.

lead.text: A different agent has a window of 200,000 tokens and is set to compact when usage reaches 75% of the window. Its context now holds 120,000 tokens. Work out how much room is left before compaction runs.

reveal.text: The trigger is at 150,000 tokens, and the agent has used 120,000 of them. Any tool result larger than 30,000 tokens will therefore start compaction on its own.

lead.text: An agent's history has grown to 30,000 tokens, and it asks the model to summarise it in 1,500 tokens. Think about what such a summary can contain, and begin by working out how much smaller it is than the history.

reveal.text: The summary is twenty times smaller than what it replaces, so it can hold the gist of the history and only a fraction of its detail. The next screen shows how to choose what the summary keeps.

steps.headline: Compaction replaces old turns with a summary, and a summary is shorter because it leaves things out.

lead.text: **Compaction** replaces the older part of the context with a summary written by the model, and keeps the most recent turns word for word. In the figure it takes the 83,000 tokens in use down to 24,000: the 8,000 of instructions stay, the old turns and results become a summary of 4,000, and the latest 12,000 tokens are kept as they were. The agent then has room for many more steps before it needs to compact again.

What a summary drops is the price of the room it frees. A summary keeps the outline of what happened and tends to lose exact values, identifiers and the reasoning behind a decision, which may be the very detail that a later step needs, so the instruction to the summariser should say what to preserve: decisions made, identifiers such as an order number, values that were quoted, and tasks still open. Anthropic's account of its multi-agent research system describes the same practice, in which agents summarise completed phases of their work and store the essential information outside the context before they move on.

steps.headline: External memory holds what must outlive the context: decisions, standing preferences and open tasks.

lead.text: Some facts cannot be left to a summary, because they have to be available exactly and in later runs as well as in this one. For these an agent has **external memory**: notes and files that it writes with one tool and reads back with another. External memory takes no room in the window until something is read from it, and it survives both compaction and the end of the run. What belongs there is what would be costly to lose: the decisions made, a user's standing preferences, the tasks still open, and the plan. Anthropic's multi-agent research system has its lead agent save its plan to memory for this reason, since its context can be truncated once it grows past 200,000 tokens, and the plan has to survive.

afterFigure.text: The figure sorts four facts into the three places a fact can live: the context, for what the current step needs; a summary, for older detail that may be lost; and the external store, for what must last. Memory differs from retrieval in one respect that matters for safety: retrieval only reads, whereas memory is also written, so a wrong note persists and is read as fact by every later run. A memory tool is a write tool in the sense of the earlier lesson, and it deserves a precise description and the same care.

reveal.text: A preference that has to outlast the run cannot rely on the context or on a summary, so the agent writes it to the store and reads it when it is relevant.

steps.headline: Work out whether a 21,000-token tool result sets off compaction in the 100,000-token window.

workedSteps.text: The agent compacts at 80% of the window, so the trigger is at 80% of 100,000 tokens.
The history before the result is 62,000 tokens. Adding the result of 21,000 tokens gives the new total.
Compare the total with the trigger: 83,000 is above 80,000, so compaction runs.
Find how far over the trigger the total is, in tokens.

steps.headline: Work out whether a result of 8,000 tokens triggers compaction in a 128,000-token window set to compact at 75%, with 90,000 tokens in use.

workedSteps.text: Find the trigger: 75% of the window.
Add the result to the history to find the new total.
Compare the total with the trigger. It is above 96,000, so compaction runs.
State how many tokens the total is over the trigger.

lead.text: The team doubles the window to 200,000 tokens and keeps the trigger at 80% of it. The history is again 62,000 tokens, and the same 21,000-token result arrives. Work out whether and how far the trigger is now from the total.

reveal.text: The larger window moves the trigger out to 160,000 tokens and puts the total, 83,000, far below it, so compaction is postponed. The postponed steps are not free, because each one re-reads the larger context, which is why a bigger window delays the problem and leaves the planning in place.

lead.text: On Monday the agent wrote this note to external memory: "Refund for order 4502 approved." On Tuesday the refund was refused after review, and nobody updated the note. On Wednesday a new session starts and reads its notes.

reveal.text: The agent has no way to know that the note is stale, so it treats the note as true. The fix lies in the write tools: a note needs an owner, a date and a way to be corrected.

lessons.orientation: Decide what an agent keeps in its context, summarises or stores outside it, and compute when compaction triggers.
lessons.nextAction: Compare the planning patterns that decide what an agent does with its steps.

blocks.text: An agent that has been running for an hour holds, in its context, every instruction it was given, the description of every tool, each turn of the conversation and every result that came back. If the window is 100,000 tokens and 62,000 are already in use, a single tool result of 21,000 tokens takes the total to 83,000, and the agent has either to throw something away or to stop. Which things to throw away, which to shorten and which to keep somewhere else is a design decision, and it is made before the run starts.
The figure draws the window to scale early in a run and later in the same run, with the point at which this agent compacts marked on it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to decide what an agent keeps in context, summarises or stores outside it, and compute the point at which compaction triggers.
intro.whyItMatters: An agent that runs long must plan its context, because the window limits what it can see and every token in it is paid for again at each step.

recap.keyIdea: An agent plans its context as a budget: it keeps what the current step needs, compacts what is old, and writes what must last to external memory.

blocks.text: The working context is a budget of tokens, and compaction is triggered when use passes a set share of the window, as a tool result of 21,000 tokens does when 62,000 are already in use in a window of 100,000. A summary frees room by losing detail, so what must survive exactly, such as decisions, preferences and open tasks, is written to external memory, where a wrong note persists and has to be treated like any other write. A bigger window postpones these decisions without removing them.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at planning patterns, the ways an agent can organise its steps before and while it takes them.

lessons.title: Planning and reasoning patterns

steps.headline: A reason-act loop decides each step after seeing the last result, which suits a task whose steps cannot be known in advance.

lead.text: A nightly export job has failed, and nobody yet knows why. The first thing to do is to read its log, and what to do second depends on what the log says, so no one could write the steps in advance. The **reason-act loop** meets this by interleaving a short reasoning step with an action and its observation: the model writes a line of reasoning, takes one action, reads the result, and reasons again with the result in front of it. Yao and colleagues introduced the pattern, called ReAct, in a 2022 paper, and reported that alternating the two worked better on interactive tasks than either reasoning alone or acting alone.

afterFigure.text: The figure follows one such run. After the log shows a full disk, the agent's next line of reasoning asks which folder is largest, and that question exists only because of what the log said. A reason-act loop therefore adapts at every step, and pays for it with one model call per step. The reasoning lines also need to be read with some care. They are text the model has written, and they help a person follow the run, but they are not a verified account of how the model reached its answer, so a sensible-looking line is not evidence that the step was right.

diagram.alt: Three stages of a reason-act run investigating a failing nightly job. After the first step the agent has read the log and seen a disk-full error. After the second it has measured disk usage and found 41 GB of 50 GB in /data/tmp. After the third it reasons that temporary files are the cause and plans to ask before clearing them.

lead.text: A failing job must be fixed, and the steps depend on what the logs show. Compare the three flows in the opening figure and decide which fits.

reveal.text: The steps cannot be written until the first result is read, so the decision has to be made again after each observation, which is what the reason-act loop does.

steps.headline: Plan then execute writes all the steps first, which is cheaper when the steps are known and brittle when an early result changes the task.

lead.text: Some tasks have steps that are known before the first action. Filing an expense claim means opening the form, entering the claimant and the amount, attaching the receipt, submitting and saving the confirmation, and none of that depends on what any step returns. For a task of this kind the agent can write the whole plan first and then carry it out, which is **plan then execute**, and it needs the model for the plan and for any step that really needs judgement, rather than for the choice of every step.

afterFigure.text: A plan is a guess about the future, and an observation can break it. In the figure the receipt is too large to attach at step 4, so the plan no longer works from that point. The agent keeps the three steps already done, notes the failed attempt, and writes a new plan from step 4 onwards, here three steps in place of the original three, so 3 steps done, 1 failed and 3 new make 7 actions in all. Plan then execute therefore works best when the steps are predictable and a failure is rare, and a task in which early observations keep changing what is needed will make the agent replan so often that a reason-act loop would have been cheaper.

diagram.alt: A six-step expense-claim plan and what happens when step 4, attaching the receipt, fails. Steps 1 to 3 are done, step 4 fails because the file is too large, and a new three-step plan replaces the rest: shrink the receipt, attach it and submit, save the confirmation. In all, 7 actions are taken.

lead.text: An agent writes an eight-step plan, and step 5 fails. It keeps steps 1 to 4, which succeeded, and writes a new four-step plan to finish the task from step 5, which it carries out in full. Count every action it took, including the failed attempt at step 5.

reveal.text: Four steps were done, one was attempted and failed, and four new steps followed, so the failure added one wasted action on top of the replanned steps.

lead.text: A form-filling task has eight steps that never change. A reason-act loop makes one model call per step. A plan-then-execute agent makes one call to write the plan and uses the model again in only two of the eight steps, because the other six are mechanical. Work out how many model calls the plan-then-execute agent makes.

reveal.text: The plan-then-execute agent makes three calls against the loop's eight, so planning first is much cheaper here. Two things limit the saving: it holds only while the plan survives, and every replan is another model call.

steps.headline: Reflection improves a result only when a check supplies a fact that the model did not already have.

lead.text: The third pattern acts on a result that has already been produced. In **reflection** the agent checks an attempt, writes a short critique of what was wrong, and tries again with the critique in its context. Shinn and colleagues describe the method in the Reflexion paper, in which an agent turns feedback from a task, such as the failures reported by unit tests, into written reflections that it keeps for the next attempt, and they report that a coding agent built this way reached 91% pass@1 on the HumanEval benchmark at a time when GPT-4 without it was reported at 80%.

afterFigure.text: The word that matters in that account is *feedback*. In the figure's first view the tests report that 2 of 20 fail, and the critique can name the cause because the test supplied it. In the second view the model is asked whether its answer is right, and it replies that it thinks so, which gives it nothing new to act on, so another attempt will probably repeat the first. Reflection is therefore only as good as its signal: a test result, a checker or a measurement is reliable, and the model's own confidence is not.

diagram.alt: Two reflection loops. With a test as the signal, the tests report 2 of 20 failing, the critique names the cause, rounding applied before tax, and the next attempt can fix it. With only the model's own opinion, the model says it thinks the answer is right and nothing new is learned.
diagram.caption: Reflection improves an answer when a check supplies a fact. Use the buttons to compare the two.

lead.text: A coding agent runs a suite of 20 tests and 5 fail. It reflects on the failures, edits the code, and runs the suite again, when 2 fail. Use the count of passing tests as the signal.

reveal.text: The tests gave the agent an outside measure, so it could tell that the second attempt was better than the first without trusting its own opinion of it.

steps.headline: Choose a pattern for filing the expense claim, using three questions about the task.

workedSteps.text: Are the steps known before the first action? Open the form, enter the details, attach the receipt, submit: they are, and they do not depend on one another's results.
Might an observation change the task? Occasionally, as when the receipt is too large, but then only the tail of the plan changes.
Is there a check that supplies a fact? Submission reports success or an error, so a failure is visible without the model's opinion.
Name the pattern that follows from these answers, writing the plan first and rewriting it on failure.

steps.headline: Choose a pattern for fixing a failing nightly job, using the same three questions.

workedSteps.text: Are the steps known before the first action? No, because they depend on what the log says.
Might an observation change the task? Yes, at every step, since each result decides what to look at next.
The first two answers rule out a plan written in advance. Name the pattern that decides each step after the last result.

lead.text: The plan-then-execute agent from the cost question makes one call for the plan and uses the model in two steps. This time a step fails, so it makes one more call to write a new plan, and the new plan again uses the model in two steps. Count the calls.

reveal.text: The agent makes six calls against the loop's eight, so most of the saving has gone. A task that fails often would lose the rest, which is the sense in which a rigid plan stops being cheaper.

lead.text: A reviewer reads a reason-act run and finds that every reasoning line looks sensible and that the final answer follows from them. The agent proposed deleting old files from a shared drive.

reveal.text: Sensible-looking reasoning is text, and a fluent account can accompany a wrong action. Before a deletion the useful evidence comes from outside the model: a listing of the files, or an approval from a person.

lessons.orientation: Choose between acting step by step, planning first and reflecting, for a given task.
lessons.nextAction: Combine model calls into chains, parallel branches and evaluator loops.

blocks.text: A nightly export job has failed and nobody knows why. The first sensible action is to read its log, and the second depends on what the log says, so the agent cannot be given its steps in advance. A different task, filing an expense claim, has steps that are known before the first action. And a third, writing code that must pass a test suite, has a result that can be checked and improved. Each of these calls for a different way of organising the agent's steps.
The figure sets out three such patterns, and this lesson takes them one at a time, with the arithmetic that shows what each costs.

diagram.alt: Three flows an agent can follow. A reason-act loop alternates reasoning, acting and observing. Plan then execute writes a plan, follows its steps and writes a new plan if a step fails. Reflection makes an attempt, checks it, writes a critique and tries again.
diagram.caption: Each flow puts the decision in a different place. Use the buttons to compare the three.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between a reason-act loop, plan then execute and reflection for a task, and count the actions or calls each takes.
intro.whyItMatters: The pattern an agent uses decides how many model calls it makes, how it recovers from a failure, and whether it can improve a result.

recap.keyIdea: Choose the reason-act loop when the steps depend on what is observed, plan then execute when the steps are known, and reflection when a check supplies a fact to learn from.

blocks.text: A reason-act loop decides each step after the last result and pays one model call for each, plan then execute writes the steps first and repairs them when an observation breaks the plan, and reflection critiques a finished attempt and retries. Planning first costs fewer calls only while the plan survives, since each replan adds a failed attempt and a new plan, and reflection helps only where a test or checker supplies a fact the model did not have. In every pattern the reasoning the model writes is text, and a sensible-looking line is not evidence that the step was right.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson combines model calls into fixed workflow patterns: chains, parallel branches and evaluator loops.

lessons.title: Composed workflow patterns

steps.headline: Chaining and routing arrange model calls in code, one after another or by classification, so the path is still fixed by the programmer.

lead.text: Anthropic's guide to building agents describes five workflow patterns, which are ways of composing model calls in code so that the path stays under the programmer's control, and the figure draws them. The simplest is **prompt chaining**, a fixed sequence of calls in which each takes the output of the one before: an outline, then a draft written from the outline, then a translation of the draft. The guide notes that a check can be placed between the calls, so that a chain stops at a step that has gone wrong.

**Routing** begins with a call that classifies the input and sends it to one of several specialised follow-ups, which suits a task that falls into distinct kinds, such as a support message that is about billing, shipping or a fault, each handled by its own prompt and tools. In both patterns the structure is fixed before the input arrives, and the model decides only what goes inside a call. The remaining three patterns relax that in different ways, and the next screens take them in turn.

A document is turned into a summary, the summary is turned into an email, and the email is checked for tone, always in that order and always using the output of the previous call. Look at the five patterns in the opening figure.

reveal.text: The order never changes and each call reads only what the last one produced, which makes the design a chain. The programmer can test each link separately.

lead.text: Three independent branches of a task each need one model call, and they take 4 seconds, 6 seconds and 5 seconds. Nothing in one branch depends on another. Estimate how long the three take if they are started at the same moment, before the next screen explains how.

reveal.text: All three run together, so the work is finished when the slowest branch is. The figure on the next screen shows why the three times are not added.

steps.headline: Parallel branches finish when the slowest one does, but they still use all the calls, so they cost the same.

lead.text: **Parallelisation** runs model calls that do not depend on one another at the same time. Anthropic's guide describes two forms: *sectioning*, in which a task is split into independent parts that run together, such as one call checking a document for factual errors while another checks it for tone, and *voting*, in which the same task is run several times to obtain several answers that are then compared. The figure draws the timeline for branches of 4, 6 and 5 seconds. Run one after another they take 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 seconds, and run at the same time they take only as long as the slowest, which is 6.

afterFigure.text: Two cautions follow. The time is the slowest branch *plus* any step that merges the results, since the merge cannot begin until the last branch has finished. And parallel branches save time and not money, because each branch is still a model call and all of them are paid for, so a parallel design is justified by latency or by the quality of the result, and not by cost. Branches that do depend on one another cannot be run in parallel at all, since one has to wait for the other's output.

diagram.alt: Two timelines for three branches taking 4, 6 and 5 seconds. Run one after another they take 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 seconds. Run at the same time they all finish when the slowest one, 6 seconds, finishes.
diagram.caption: The axis is in seconds. Use the buttons to compare running the branches in sequence and at once.

lead.text: A document is checked in three independent sections that take 7, 3 and 9 seconds when run at the same moment. A merge step, which cannot begin until all three have finished, then takes 2 seconds. Use what the last screen said about the merge.

reveal.text: Run in sequence, the same work would take 7 + 3 + 9 + 2 = 21 seconds, so running the branches together saves 10 seconds, though the merge stays on the critical path.

steps.headline: A majority vote helps only when the voters are independent and each is right more often than not.

lead.text: Voting runs the same task several times and takes the answer that most runs agree on. Suppose three independent voters are each right with probability *p*, and the majority wins. The majority is right if all three are right, which has probability p³, or if exactly two are, and there are three ways to choose which two, each with probability p² × (1 − p). The chance that the majority is right is therefore 3p²(1 − p) + p³.

For p = 0.8 this is 3 × 0.64 × 0.2 + 0.512 = 0.384 + 0.512 = 0.896, so the vote lifts an 80% voter to about 90%. The formula also shows when voting fails to help. At p = 0.5 the majority is right half the time, no better than one voter, and at p = 0.4 it falls to 0.352, *worse* than one voter. The calculation also assumes independence, and voters that are the same model with the same prompt tend to make the same mistakes, so the real gain is smaller than the formula suggests.

diagram.alt: Bars comparing one voter with a majority of three independent voters. With voters right 80 percent of the time the majority is right 0.896. At 50 percent the majority is right 0.5. At 40 percent it falls to 0.352, worse than one voter.

steps.headline: Find the chance that a majority of three independent voters is right when each is right 70% of the time.

workedSteps.text: The majority is right if all three are right or exactly two are. Write the chance of each case, using p = 0.7 and 1 − p = 0.3.
Exactly two right: there are three ways to choose the two, and each has probability 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.3.
All three right: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7.
Add the two cases to find the chance that the majority is right.

steps.headline: Find the chance that a majority of three independent voters is right when each is right 60% of the time.

workedSteps.text: Use the same two cases, with p = 0.6 and 1 − p = 0.4. Exactly two right gives three ways, each 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.4.
All three right: 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6.
Add the two cases to find the chance that the majority is right.

steps.headline: An orchestrator chooses the subtasks after reading the input, and an evaluator loop repeats until a critic accepts.

lead.text: The fourth pattern, **orchestrator-workers**, handles the case in which the subtasks cannot be listed in advance. A central model reads the input, decides what subtasks it needs, hands each to a worker and combines the results. In the figure the task is to update a library call across a codebase, and the number of files to edit depends on the codebase: two for the first input and four for the second. The sectioning of the last screens could not express that, because it divides a task into parts that the programmer chose before the input arrived. An orchestrator is therefore more than a larger prompt, since the structure of the work is decided at run time, which is the point at which a workflow begins to resemble an agent.

The fifth, the **evaluator-optimiser**, pairs a call that proposes an answer with a call that critiques it, and repeats the pair until the evaluator accepts. It suits a task with clear criteria that a critic can apply, such as a translation checked against a style guide, and it is the workflow form of the reflection pattern from the last lesson. Each round adds two calls of latency, so the loop needs a limit on the number of rounds, for the same reason as the step budget.

diagram.alt: Two inputs to the same orchestrator. A codebase needing 2 edits leads the orchestrator to start 2 workers. A codebase needing 4 edits leads it to start 4. The number of subtasks is decided after reading the input.
