answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inputs are 2,000, 2,500, 3,000, 3,500 and 4,000, and their sum is 15,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps the context at 2,000 tokens for all five steps. It grows by 500 each step.
That is the input to the last step only.

questions.prompt: Each step of a run succeeds with probability 0.95, independently, and the run needs all 10 steps to succeed. What is the chance that it does, to two decimal places?
hints: The run succeeds only if every step succeeds.
Raise 0.95 to the power 10 on a calculator.
Round to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: Ten steps that are each 95% reliable finish only about 60% of the time, because the chances multiply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.95 multiplied by itself 10 times is about 0.5987, which is 0.60 to two places.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for a single step. All ten must succeed.
That is the chance that a single step fails.
That is the chance that the run fails. The question asks for the chance that it succeeds.

questions.prompt: What is a hard limit on the iterations, tokens or time of an agent run called?
hints: It is enforced by the code around the model, not by the model.
Its name says what it limits and what kind of allowance it is.
questions.onCorrect: Because the code enforces it, a step budget ends the loop even when the model never decides to stop.

misconceptions.feedback: A final answer ends a run only if the model decides to write one, and a limit is needed for the case where it does not.

questions.prompt: Which description will let the model use the refund tool correctly?
hints: Look for the description that says when to use the tool and what each input is.
Which description would still be usable by someone who has never seen the tool's code?
questions.onCorrect: A usable description says when to call the tool, where each input comes from, and what the result looks like.

acceptedIdeas: "issue_refund: Pays money back for one order. Use after read_policy shows the order is eligible. Inputs: order_id from search_orders, amount_cents up to the order total, idempotency_key. Returns a refund id or an error code."
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: "issue_refund: Pays money back for one order. Use after read_policy shows the order is eligible. Inputs: order_id from search_orders, amount_cents up to the order total, idempotency_key. Returns a refund id or an error code."

choices.label: "refund: Refunds a customer."
"issue_refund: A powerful tool for everything to do with refunds. Use it whenever a customer is unhappy."

"issue_refund: Pays money back for one order. Use after read_policy shows the order is eligible. Inputs: order_id from search_orders, amount_cents up to the order total, idempotency_key. Returns a refund id or an error code."

misconceptions.feedback: Four words leave the model to guess what to pass, when to call the tool and what comes back.
A description that invites use whenever a customer is unhappy sends the model to issue refunds that the policy does not allow.

questions.prompt: Is cancel_subscription a read tool or a write tool? Answer with one word, read or write.
hints: Ask whether the shop is the same after the call as before it.
A tool that ends a plan changes a record.
questions.onCorrect: A tool that changes a record outside the conversation is a write tool, and that is true of any tool that cancels, creates, sends or pays.

misconceptions.feedback: A read tool leaves everything as it was. Cancelling a plan changes what the customer is billed.

questions.prompt: How many refunds does the customer receive?
hints: Each call that reached the server did something.
The first call succeeded even though the agent never saw the reply.
Count the calls that reached the server.
questions.onCorrect: A write tool with no memory of earlier calls treats every request as new, so a retry after a lost reply pays again.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first call succeeded and the two retries each reached the server, and a tool with no way to recognise a repeat pays out on every call, so there are 3 refunds.

misconceptions.feedback: One refund was due, but the tool pays on every call that reaches it, and all three did.
That counts only the two retries. The first call also paid out.

questions.prompt: How many refunds did the server make?
hints: A refund is made only when the server sees a key for the first time.
The calls used two different keys.
Count the distinct keys.
questions.onCorrect: The number of refunds equals the number of distinct keys, however many times each is sent.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the first call with each distinct key makes a refund: keys a and b, so 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every call. Calls that repeat a stored key make no refund.
The calls carry only two distinct keys, a and b.

questions.prompt: How many of the two refunds does the server actually make?
hints: Check whether the two calls carry the same key or different keys.
The server makes a refund only the first time it sees a key.
The two calls here carry one key between them.
questions.onCorrect: A key that is shared by two different actions makes the server treat the second as a retry of the first, and the second action is silently dropped.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both calls carry refund-4471. The first makes a refund, and the second is treated as a repeat of it, so only 1 refund is made.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the two refunds as different, but they carry the same key, so the server takes the second for a repeat.
The first call carries a key the server has not seen, so it makes a refund.

questions.prompt: Which of these tools is a write tool?
hints: Ask which tool leaves something behind when it is called.
Three of the four only fetch information.
questions.onCorrect: issue_refund moves money out of the shop, which cannot be taken back by calling another tool.

choices.label: search_orders
get_customer
issue_refund
read_policy

misconceptions.feedback: search_orders only fetches orders, and the shop is unchanged after any number of calls.
get_customer only fetches a record and leaves it as it was.
read_policy only fetches policy text.

questions.prompt: A refund call carrying the same idempotency key is sent 3 times. How many refunds happen?
hints: The server remembers every key it has seen.
Only the first call with a given key does anything.
The three calls share one key.
questions.onCorrect: The key lets the server tell the retries from a new request, so one intended refund is made once however often it is sent.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The server makes a refund for the first call and returns the stored result to the other two, so 1 refund is made.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of calls. With a key, only the first makes a refund.
That counts the repeats. They are the calls that make no refund.

questions.prompt: What is the caller-supplied token called that lets a server treat a repeated request as one?
hints: It identifies one intended action, and the caller sends it with every attempt.
Its name says that repeating the operation has the same effect as doing it once.
questions.onCorrect: The server stores the key with the first result and answers later requests with the same key from that record.

misconceptions.feedback: A retry is what the key makes safe, but the token itself has a different name.

questions.prompt: How many separate integrations are needed?
hints: Each application needs a connection to every tool.
That is 6 integrations for each application.
Multiply the number of applications by the number of tools.
questions.onCorrect: Without a shared protocol the work grows as the product of the two numbers, which is why a common format pays off quickly.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 4 applications needs its own integration with each of the 6 tools, and 4 × 6 = 24.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 4 + 6, the count with a shared protocol. Without one, every application needs its own link to every tool.
That is the number of tools. Each of the four applications needs a link to each of them.
That is the number of applications. Each needs a link to every tool.

questions.prompt: Which of the three roles, host, client or server, runs the tool?
hints: The model chooses the tool, and the client carries the message.
One role offers the tools and holds their code.
questions.onCorrect: The server holds the tool's code, so it is the part that does the work when a call arrives.

misconceptions.feedback: The host contains the model, which chooses the tool, but the tool's code lives in another role.
The client sends the call and holds the connection, and it does not run the tool.

questions.prompt: In a JSON-RPC request, which key names the operation to perform?
hints: The key is a word that names what is being asked for, not who is asking.
In the message above, its value is tools/list.
questions.onCorrect: The value of method is the operation, such as tools/list or tools/call, and params carries its inputs.

misconceptions.feedback: The id pairs a reply with its request, and it does not say what to do.
The params hold the inputs. The operation itself is named by another key.

questions.prompt: Which transport does a host use to talk to a local server that it starts as a subprocess? Give the short name.
hints: A program already has a place where it reads input and a place where it writes output.
The short name is built from standard, input and output.
questions.onCorrect: The host writes to the server's standard input and reads its standard output, which needs no network at all.

misconceptions.feedback: HTTP is the transport for remote servers. A program on the same machine can use a simpler channel.
MCP defines two transports, and a socket is not either of them.

questions.prompt: What id must the reply carry?
hints: The id pairs a reply with its request.
Look at the id in the request.
The reply repeats it.
questions.onCorrect: The id is the only link between a request and its reply, which lets a client send several requests before any of them is answered.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The reply answers the request by carrying the request's id, and the request's id is 7.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the id from the tools/list request on an earlier screen. Read the id in this tools/call request.
That is part of the customer identifier c-42, which is an argument and not the id.

questions.prompt: How many fewer pieces of work does the shared protocol need than the bespoke integrations?
hints: Work out the bespoke count as a product and the protocol count as a sum.
The bespoke count is 6 × 9 and the protocol count is 6 + 9.
Subtract the second from the first.
questions.onCorrect: The saving grows quickly with the numbers, because a product grows much faster than a sum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Bespoke integrations: 6 × 9 = 54. Shared protocol: 6 + 9 = 15. The difference is 54 − 15 = 39.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of bespoke integrations alone. The question asks for the difference.
That is the number with a shared protocol, and the question asks how many fewer it needs.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of protocol and job is right?
hints: Ask which of the two is a tool and which is an agent that decides for itself.
One of these protocols connects agents to tools and data.
questions.onCorrect: A tool server runs what it is told and an agent decides for itself, which is the line between MCP and A2A.

acceptedIdeas: A2A for the delivery dispute and MCP for the order database
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A2A for the delivery dispute and MCP for the order database

choices.label: A2A for the delivery dispute and MCP for the order database
MCP for the delivery dispute and A2A for the order database
MCP for both, since both involve calling something
A2A for both, since the courier agent will call the shop

misconceptions.feedback: The order database is a plain tool, and the courier's agent decides for itself, so the two are the wrong way round.
MCP treats the other side as a tool server, and the courier's agent plans and decides for itself.
The order database is a tool and has no goals of its own, which is what MCP serves.

questions.prompt: 5 applications and 8 tool servers share a protocol. How many implementations of the protocol are needed in total?
hints: Each application implements the protocol once, and so does each server.
Add the number of applications to the number of servers.
questions.onCorrect: With a shared protocol the work grows as a sum, where bespoke wiring would need 5 × 8 = 40 integrations.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 5 applications implements the client side once and each of the 8 servers implements the server side once, which makes 5 + 8 = 13.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of bespoke integrations. With a shared protocol each side implements it once.
That counts only the servers. The applications implement the client side as well.

questions.prompt: In the JSON-RPC response {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "result": {...}}, which key links the response to the request it answers?
hints: The reply repeats a value from the request.
The key is a two-letter word.
questions.onCorrect: The id is the only link between a request and its reply, so a reply that repeats it can be matched even when several requests are in flight.

misconceptions.feedback: The method names the operation in a request. The reply is matched to its request by another key.
The jsonrpc member only gives the protocol version, which is the same in every message.

questions.prompt: What is the channel that carries MCP messages between a client and a server called?
hints: MCP defines two of them: standard input and output for a local server, and HTTP for a remote one.
The word names what carries the messages, not the messages themselves.
questions.onCorrect: Because the protocol defines the messages separately from the channel, the same server logic can be reached over stdio or over HTTP.

misconceptions.feedback: The protocol and the message format are what travels. The channel that carries them has a different name.

questions.prompt: How many more tokens can be added before compaction triggers?
hints: Find the token count at which compaction triggers.
75% of 200,000 tokens is the trigger.
Subtract the tokens already in use from the trigger.
questions.onCorrect: Compaction is triggered by a count of tokens, which is why a single large tool result can set it off at any step.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the room left in the whole window, 200,000 − 120,000. Compaction triggers earlier, at 75% usage.
That is the trigger point. The question asks how much room is left before it.
That is 25% of the window. The trigger is at 75% of it.

questions.prompt: How many times smaller than the history is the summary?
hints: Compare the two sizes by division.
Divide the history by the summary.
questions.onCorrect: A summary twenty times smaller has room for the outline of the history and for little of its exact detail.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30,000 ÷ 1,500 = 20, so the summary is one twentieth of the size.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of tokens saved. The question asks how many times smaller the summary is, which is a ratio.
That is the summary as a fraction of the history. Divide the other way for how many times smaller.

questions.prompt: What is the process of replacing old turns with a model-written summary, to free room in the context, called?
hints: The agent is set to do it when usage reaches a threshold.
The name comes from making the context more compact.
questions.onCorrect: Compaction frees room by trading old detail for a summary, so it is set to run before the window is full.

misconceptions.feedback: Writing a summary is part of it. The name for replacing old turns with one, to free room, is different.

questions.prompt: Where should the agent keep the user's standing preference for metric units?
hints: The preference has to last beyond this session.
Ask which place survives compaction and the end of the run, without filling the window.
questions.onCorrect: External memory outlives the run and takes room in the window only when it is read.

acceptedIdeas: In external memory, read when it is relevant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In external memory, read when it is relevant

choices.label: In an old turn of the conversation
Added to every prompt as the whole of the past chat
In external memory, read when it is relevant
Nowhere, because the user will repeat it

misconceptions.feedback: An old turn is the first thing compaction summarises, and a session ends with it, so the preference could vanish.
Adding the whole past chat to every prompt would fill the window and make every step dearer.
The point of external memory is that the user need not repeat a preference every session.

questions.prompt: By how many tokens does the total exceed the trigger?
hints: Subtract the trigger from the new total.
The total is 83,000 and the trigger is 80,000.
questions.onCorrect: The total passes the trigger by 3,000 tokens, so compaction runs at this step, even though the window itself still has 17,000 tokens free.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the room left in the whole window. The question compares the total with the trigger.
That is the size of the tool result, not how far past the trigger the total goes.

questions.prompt: By how many tokens does the new total exceed the trigger?
hints: Use the new total and the trigger from the lines above.
The total is 98,000 and the trigger is 96,000.
Subtract the trigger from the total.
questions.onCorrect: Even a modest result of 8,000 tokens can trigger compaction when the history already sits close to the trigger.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the room below the trigger before the result was added. The question asks by how much the new total exceeds it.
That is the room left in the whole window after the result, not the excess over the trigger.

questions.prompt: How many more tokens can be added after the result before compaction triggers?
hints: Find the new trigger from the new window.
The trigger is 80% of 200,000 tokens, and the total after the result is 83,000.
Subtract the total from the trigger.
questions.onCorrect: A bigger window moves the trigger out and delays compaction, while every step still pays to re-read what has accumulated.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the room under the old trigger at 100,000. The window and trigger are now larger.
That is the room in the whole window after the result. The trigger is at 80% of it.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely result on Wednesday?
hints: Think about what the agent can know about the note beyond its text.
Memory has writes, and nothing in the note says that it has changed.
questions.onCorrect: A memory that is written to can hold a wrong or stale fact, and every later run reads it as though it were true.

acceptedIdeas: The agent treats the note as true and may act on it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The agent treats the note as true and may act on it

choices.label: The note is ignored, because old notes are always discarded
The agent treats the note as true and may act on it
The note is corrected automatically when the session starts
The agent asks the model whether the note is current, and the model knows

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the store discards a note because of its age, and the agent will read it when it is relevant.
Nothing in the example updates the note, and the store does not know that the refund was refused.
The model has only the note and its context, so it has no way to know that the review changed the outcome.

questions.prompt: A window holds 128,000 tokens and the agent compacts at 80% usage. The context holds 85,000 tokens. How many more tokens can be added before compaction triggers?
hints: Find the trigger as a number of tokens.
80% of 128,000 is the trigger.
Subtract the tokens in use from it.
questions.onCorrect: The trigger is a token count, so the room left is the difference between it and the tokens already in use.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the room in the whole window, 128,000 − 85,000. Compaction triggers at 80% of the window.
That is the trigger point. The question asks for the room left before it.

questions.prompt: A history of 24,000 tokens is compacted into a summary of 1,500 tokens. How many times smaller is the summary?
hints: Compare the two sizes by division.
Divide the history by the summary.
questions.onCorrect: A summary sixteen times smaller keeps the outline and gives up much of the detail.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of tokens saved. The question asks how many times smaller the summary is.
That is the summary as a fraction of the history. Divide the other way.

questions.prompt: What do we call the notes and files that an agent writes and reads back by tool, outside its context?
hints: It lives outside the window and survives the end of a run.
Its name says where it is kept.
questions.onCorrect: Because it lives outside the context, external memory costs no room until something is read back from it.

misconceptions.feedback: The context is what is in the prompt on this step. The notes kept outside it have another name.
A summary lives inside the context. The notes kept outside it have another name.

questions.prompt: The steps to fix a failing job are unknown until its logs have been read. Which pattern fits best?
hints: Ask whether the first step can be chosen without any result in hand.
Which pattern chooses each step after seeing the result of the last one?
questions.onCorrect: When the next step depends on the last result, deciding step by step is what makes the task tractable.

choices.label: A fixed plan written before the first action
Reflection with no outside check
The reason-act loop
No tools, only a long prompt

misconceptions.feedback: A plan written first would have to guess what the logs show, and the first observation would probably contradict it.
Reflection critiques a finished attempt, and without a check it has no new fact to work from.
Without tools the model cannot read the logs, so it cannot find the cause.

questions.prompt: How many actions did the agent take in total?
hints: Count the actions in three groups: done before the failure, the failed attempt, and the new plan.
That is 4, then 1, then 4.
Add the three groups.
questions.onCorrect: A failed attempt still counts as an action taken, so a replan costs the failure plus the steps of the new plan.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Steps 1 to 4 are 4 actions, the failed attempt at step 5 is 1, and the new plan adds 4, so 4 + 1 + 4 = 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That is either the length of the original plan or the count without the failed attempt. Count the done steps, the failed attempt and the new plan separately.
That counts the steps up to and including the failure only. The new four-step plan was carried out as well.

questions.prompt: How many model calls does the plan-then-execute agent make?
hints: Count the call that writes the plan separately from the calls inside steps.
The plan is one call, and two of the eight steps use the model.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: Writing the plan once replaces the per-step choice, so the number of calls follows the number of steps that need judgement.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One call writes the plan and two steps use the model, so 1 + 2 = 3 calls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reason-act loop's count, one call per step. This agent calls the model only for the plan and for two steps.
That counts the steps that use the model but leaves out the call that wrote the plan.

questions.prompt: How many more tests pass after the second attempt than after the first?
hints: Work out how many pass in each run.
The first run has 15 passing and the second 18.
Subtract the first from the second.
questions.onCorrect: A count of passing tests is a signal that does not depend on what the model believes about its own work.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first run has 20 − 5 = 15 passing and the second 20 − 2 = 18, and 18 − 15 = 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number failing after the second attempt. Compare how many pass in each run.
That is the number failing at the start. The question asks how many more pass the second time.

questions.prompt: Which pattern writes the plan first and rewrites it when a step fails?
hints: The steps are known in advance, and the agent replans only on failure.
The pattern is named after what it does first and what it does second.
questions.onCorrect: Predictable steps are what make a plan written first worth its cost, and failures are handled by rewriting its tail.

misconceptions.feedback: A reason-act loop decides each step after the last result, whereas the claim's steps are known in advance.
Reflection critiques a finished attempt. This pattern writes the steps before any attempt.

questions.prompt: Which pattern decides each step after the last result?
hints: The pattern interleaves a short reasoning step with an action and an observation.
It is also known by the name of the 2022 paper that introduced it.
questions.onCorrect: When every observation can change what to do next, a plan written first would be out of date after one step.

misconceptions.feedback: A plan written first would be out of date as soon as the first log line is read.
Reflection critiques a result that already exists. This task has no result yet.

questions.prompt: How many model calls does the agent make in total?
hints: Count the calls for the first plan and its steps, then the calls for the new plan and its steps.
Each plan costs 1 call, and then 2 steps use the model.
Add the two groups of calls.
questions.onCorrect: Each replan costs a plan call and further model steps, so frequent failures erode the saving that planning first provides.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first plan is 1 call and 2 steps use the model, which is 3. The new plan is 1 call and 2 more steps, which is 3, and 3 + 3 = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for one plan and its steps. The agent also wrote a second plan.
That counts two plan calls and two model steps, but the new plan again uses the model in two steps.

questions.prompt: What can the reviewer conclude about whether the proposal is right?
hints: The reasoning lines are written by the model, in the same way as its answer.
Ask what outside fact would show that the files are safe to delete.
questions.onCorrect: A reasoning line helps a reader follow a run, but it is not a verified account of how the model reached the action.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing yet, because the reasoning is text the model wrote and the proposal needs a check from outside the model
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing yet, because the reasoning is text the model wrote and the proposal needs a check from outside the model

choices.label: Nothing yet, because the reasoning is text the model wrote and the proposal needs a check from outside the model
That it is right, because every line of reasoning was sound
That it is right, because longer reasoning is more reliable
That it is wrong, because reasoning shown to a reader is usually a cover for a guess

misconceptions.feedback: The lines look sound, but they are text the model produced, and fluent text can accompany a wrong step.
Length does not make reasoning more reliable. Only a check against an outside fact does that.
The lines are not shown to be a cover for a guess. They simply are not verified evidence.

questions.prompt: An agent writes a ten-step plan, and step 7 fails. It keeps steps 1 to 6 and writes a new two-step plan that it carries out in full. Counting the failed attempt, how many actions did it take in total?
hints: Count the done steps, the failed attempt and the new plan separately.
That is 6, then 1, then 2.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: The total is the steps done before the failure, the failed attempt and the steps of the new plan.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Steps 1 to 6 are 6 actions, the failed attempt at step 7 is 1, and the new plan adds 2, so 6 + 1 + 2 = 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length of the original plan. The agent stopped after step 7 and added a new plan.
That leaves out the failed attempt at step 7.

questions.prompt: Which pattern has the agent write the critique of a finished attempt and try again with it in context?
hints: It acts on a result that already exists, not on a plan or on the next step.
Its signal should come from outside the model, such as a test.
questions.onCorrect: Reflection is reliable only when a check, such as a test, supplies the fact that the critique rests on.

misconceptions.feedback: A reason-act loop chooses the next step. Critiquing a finished attempt is a different pattern.
Plan then execute writes steps before any attempt exists.

questions.prompt: A twelve-step task is run by a reason-act loop, which makes one model call per step. A plan-then-execute agent makes one call for the plan and uses the model in 3 of the 12 steps. How many fewer calls does the plan-then-execute agent make?
hints: Count the calls each agent makes.
The loop makes 12, and the other agent makes 1 plus 3.
Subtract the smaller count from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: Planning first saves calls in proportion to the number of mechanical steps, as long as the plan survives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The loop makes 12 calls and the plan-then-execute agent makes 1 + 3 = 4, so 12 − 4 = 8 fewer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of calls the plan-then-execute agent makes. The question asks how many fewer it makes.
That counts only the 3 model steps against the 12 and forgets the call that writes the plan.

questions.prompt: Which pattern runs a fixed sequence of model calls, each using the previous call's output?
hints: The order of the calls is fixed in code.
The name says what is linked.
questions.onCorrect: In a chain the output of each call becomes the input of the next, so the whole sequence is as predictable as its links.

misconceptions.feedback: Routing sends the input to one of several specialists. In this task every call runs, in the same order.
An orchestrator chooses subtasks after reading the input, but here the sequence is fixed.

questions.prompt: How long, in seconds, does the parallel version take?
hints: Branches that run together overlap in time.
The work is done when the last branch finishes.
Find the longest of the three times.
questions.onCorrect: Parallel branches overlap, so the elapsed time is set by the slowest branch rather than by the sum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The branches run together, so the total is the longest of 4, 6 and 5, which is 6 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time if the branches ran one after another. Run together, they overlap.
That is the average of the three times. The work waits for the slowest branch.

questions.prompt: How long does the whole task take, in seconds?
hints: The merge waits for the slowest branch.
The slowest branch takes 9 seconds.
Add the merge time to it.
questions.onCorrect: The merge adds to the slowest branch because it cannot start until every branch has finished.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The branches finish when the slowest does, at 9 seconds, and the merge then takes 2 more, so 9 + 2 = 11 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time with every step in sequence. The three branches overlap.
That is the slowest branch alone. The merge step comes after it.

questions.prompt: What is the chance that the majority is right? Give it as a decimal.
hints: Add the probability of exactly two right to the probability of all three right.
The two cases are 0.441 and 0.343.
questions.onCorrect: A 70% voter becomes a 78.4% majority, a smaller gain than the 80% voter received, because the gain from voting grows with the voters' accuracy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one voter's chance. The question asks for the majority of three.
That is only the exactly-two case. Add the chance that all three are right.

questions.prompt: What is the chance that the majority is right? Give it as a decimal.
hints: Add the two cases.
The cases are 0.432 and 0.216.
questions.onCorrect: Voters at 60% give a majority at 64.8%, so voting still helps when the voters are only a little better than chance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one voter's chance. Add the two cases for the majority.
That is only the exactly-two case. Add the chance that all three are right.

questions.prompt: A subtask list that cannot be known until the input is read is best served by
hints: Ask which pattern lets the subtasks be decided at run time.
A fixed set of branches or steps is written before the input arrives.
questions.onCorrect: An orchestrator decides the subtasks at run time, which a fixed workflow cannot, since its structure is written in advance.

choices.label: Prompt chaining
Routing
Orchestrator-workers
Sectioning

misconceptions.feedback: A chain has a fixed sequence of calls, so it cannot grow or shrink with the input.
Routing picks one of several fixed specialists, and it does not create subtasks.
Sectioning splits a task into parts that the programmer chose before the input arrived.

questions.prompt: How long does the whole loop take, in seconds?
hints: Work out the time of one round, a proposal and a critique.
One round takes 3 + 2 seconds.
Multiply by the number of rounds.
questions.onCorrect: The calls in a round depend on each other and the rounds depend on each other, so nothing overlaps and the times add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each round takes 3 + 2 = 5 seconds, and three rounds take 3 × 5 = 15 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time of one round. The loop runs three rounds.
That counts only the three proposals. The evaluator's 2 seconds in each round count as well.

questions.prompt: What does the vote achieve?
hints: Ask whether the five outputs can differ.
The formula for a majority assumes independent mistakes.
questions.onCorrect: A vote helps only when the voters' errors are independent, and identical copies of one answer repeat the same error.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing, because five identical outputs are one answer repeated and the voters are not independent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing, because five identical outputs are one answer repeated and the voters are not independent

choices.label: It raises the accuracy, as it would for five independent voters
Nothing, because five identical outputs are one answer repeated and the voters are not independent
It lowers the accuracy, because every voter is wrong more often when there are more of them
It makes the answer faster, because the voters run in parallel

misconceptions.feedback: The formula assumes independent mistakes, and five identical outputs are not independent.
Adding voters does not make each one less accurate. Identical outputs simply add nothing.
Parallel voters take the time of the slowest, but they also cost five calls, and the vote still adds no accuracy here.

questions.prompt: Three independent branches take 5 s, 8 s and 6 s. How long does the parallel version take, in seconds, before any merge?
hints: Parallel branches overlap in time.
The work is finished when the slowest branch finishes.
Find the longest of 5, 8 and 6.
questions.onCorrect: Elapsed time is set by the slowest branch, while the cost is still the sum of all the calls.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The branches run together and the work waits for the slowest, which is 8 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time with the branches in sequence, 5 + 8 + 6.
That is the middle time. The work waits for the slowest branch.

questions.prompt: Three independent voters are each right 80% of the time, and the majority wins. What is the chance that the majority is right?
hints: The majority is right if exactly two voters are right or all three are.
Exactly two: 3 × 0.8² × 0.2. All three: 0.8³.
Add the two probabilities.
questions.onCorrect: Voting lifts three 80% voters to about 90%, provided the voters make independent mistakes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The majority is right with probability 3 × 0.8² × 0.2 + 0.8³ = 0.384 + 0.512 = 0.896.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one voter's chance. The question asks for the majority of three.
That is the chance that all three are right. Add the chance that exactly two are.

questions.prompt: Which pattern pairs a call that proposes an answer with a call that critiques it, repeating until the critic accepts?
hints: One call produces and another judges.
The pattern is named after the two roles.
questions.onCorrect: The loop ends when the evaluator accepts, and each round adds both calls to the latency.

misconceptions.feedback: An orchestrator splits a task into subtasks at run time. This pattern repeats a propose and critique pair.
Routing sends the input to one specialist. It does not critique an answer.

questions.prompt: What is the total number of tokens used, in thousands?
hints: Count the lead's two stages and the workers separately.
The workers use 4 × 20 thousand tokens.
Add the plan, the workers and the synthesis.
questions.onCorrect: Every worker's tokens count towards the cost, so the total grows with the number of workers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The plan is 10, the four workers use 4 × 20 = 80, and the synthesis is 10, so 10 + 80 + 10 = 100 thousand.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the workers. The lead's plan and synthesis cost 20 thousand more.
That counts the lead's stages and two workers only. There are four workers.
That leaves out two workers. All four are paid for.

questions.prompt: How many times as many tokens does the multi-agent run use as the single agent? Give it to one decimal place.
hints: Divide the multi-agent total by the single agent's total.
Both are in thousands of tokens, so the units cancel.
questions.onCorrect: The comparison is a ratio of totals, and it should be set against what the extra tokens buy in time and quality.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 ÷ 35 is about 2.857, which is 2.9 to one decimal place.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many thousand tokens more the multi-agent run uses. The question asks for a ratio.
That divides the single agent's total by the multi-agent total. Put the multi-agent total on top.

questions.prompt: How many times smaller is the summary than the pages the worker read?
hints: Compare the two sizes by division.
Divide the size of the pages by the size of the summary.
questions.onCorrect: A summary thirty times smaller is a good deal of compression, and anything it leaves out is gone from the lead's view.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of tokens saved. The question asks how many times smaller the summary is.
That is the summary as a fraction of the pages. Divide the other way.

questions.prompt: Why give a subagent a narrow context?
hints: Think about what the worker's tokens are spent on, and what enters the lead's context.
A narrow context changes what is in the prompt, and it does not change the model.
questions.onCorrect: A narrow context keeps the worker on its own task and keeps the lead's context from filling with material the lead does not need.

acceptedIdeas: It keeps the task focused and the main context small
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps the task focused and the main context small

choices.label: It makes the model smarter
It is required by the protocol
It keeps the task focused and the main context small
It lowers the temperature

misconceptions.feedback: A narrow context does not change the model. It changes what the model has in front of it.
No protocol requires it. It is a design choice with the benefits above.
Temperature is a sampling setting, unrelated to how much context an agent holds.

questions.prompt: How many of the three claims meet the contract?
hints: Check each claim for both required fields.
Claim B has no source_url.
Count the claims that pass.
questions.onCorrect: A claim with no source cannot be checked by the lead, so the schema rejects it at the boundary.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Claims A and C have both a text and a source_url, and B has no source_url, so 2 meet the contract.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every claim. Claim B has no source_url, so it does not meet the contract.
Two of the three claims have both required fields.

questions.prompt: What is the total, in thousands of tokens?
hints: Add the three stages.
The stages are 8, 45 and 7 thousand.
questions.onCorrect: The total is the lead's two stages plus the workers' combined tokens, so it is dominated by the workers when there are many.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 + 45 + 7 = 60 thousand tokens.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the workers only. The lead's plan and synthesis cost 15 thousand more.
That is the sum 8 + 7 and omits the workers.

questions.prompt: What is the likely outcome, and what is the remedy?
hints: Think about what happens when two writers each start from the same version of a file.
The contract should say who may write.
questions.onCorrect: Shared mutable state needs an owner, because two writers that start from the same version can overwrite each other's work.

acceptedIdeas: One write may overwrite the other, so give the notes a single owner who merges the workers' results
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One write may overwrite the other, so give the notes a single owner who merges the workers' results

choices.label: Both sets of findings are kept, because the agents coordinate by chat
One write may overwrite the other, so give the notes a single owner who merges the workers' results
The file grows without limit, so give each worker a larger budget
Nothing goes wrong, because the workers use different models

misconceptions.feedback: Chat between agents does not make two writes to one file safe, and neither agent sees the other's change in time.
A larger budget does not change what happens when two writes collide.
The models make no difference. The fault lies in the two concurrent writes to one file.

questions.prompt: A lead spends 8 thousand tokens planning, five workers use 12 thousand each, and the synthesis uses 12 thousand. What is the total, in thousands of tokens?
hints: Count the lead's two stages and the workers separately.
The workers use 5 × 12 thousand tokens.
Add the plan, the workers and the synthesis.
questions.onCorrect: Each added worker adds its whole token use, so the total grows with the number of workers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The plan is 8, the five workers use 5 × 12 = 60, and the synthesis is 12, so 8 + 60 + 12 = 80 thousand.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the workers. The plan and synthesis add 20 thousand.
That is the lead's two stages. The five workers add 60 thousand.

questions.prompt: Which part of an agent contract states the exact shape of what a worker returns?
hints: The contract has four fields: input, tools allowed, budget and this one.
It lets the lead check a message at the boundary.
questions.onCorrect: With an output schema the lead can reject a malformed result immediately, instead of finding the fault during synthesis.

misconceptions.feedback: The input says what goes to the worker. The shape of what comes back is another field.
The budget limits tokens and tool calls. The shape of the reply is another field.
The tool list says what the worker may call. The shape of its reply is another field.

questions.prompt: What is the name for giving a subagent only the context its task needs?
hints: The worker's context holds its brief and its own searches only.
The name says what is kept apart from what.
questions.onCorrect: Isolation keeps the worker focused and the lead's context small, and it makes the quality of the brief the lead's responsibility.

misconceptions.feedback: A handoff passes control of the conversation to another agent. Giving a worker only what it needs has a different name.
Compaction summarises old turns inside one context. This is about what each agent holds in the first place.

questions.prompt: Which action should the agent never be able to do alone?
hints: Ask which action cannot be undone and harms someone if it is wrong.
Three of these only fetch or propose.
questions.onCorrect: A permanent action that harms a customer when wrong is withheld from the agent, or put behind a person's decision.

choices.label: Search orders
Read a policy
Delete a customer account
Draft an email

misconceptions.feedback: Searching only reads, and a wrong search costs a call.
Reading a policy changes nothing.
A draft is a proposal that nobody has sent, so a person can correct it before it matters.

questions.prompt: Where must the refund limit be enforced: in the system prompt, in the user's browser, or on which other side of the path? Answer with the place that executes the tool.
hints: The place that holds the limit must be one that the model cannot change by what it writes.
It is the component that runs the tool and checks each call before it runs.
questions.onCorrect: A check in the code that runs the tool applies to every call, whatever the model wrote and however it was persuaded.

acceptedAlternatives: the server that executes the tool
the server that runs the tool

misconceptions.feedback: A prompt is text that the model reads, and a model can disregard it, so a limit placed there is only a request.
A browser belongs to the user and can be altered, so it cannot enforce a limit against a mistaken agent.

questions.prompt: How many minutes of approving is that per day, to one decimal place?
hints: Find the total number of seconds first.
1,000 approvals at 5 seconds each.
Divide the seconds by 60.
questions.onCorrect: A day of approvals adds up to well over an hour of pure clicking, which is more attention than a person can give.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000 × 5 s = 5,000 s, and 5,000 ÷ 60 is about 83.3 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total in seconds. The question asks for minutes.
That is the number of hours. The question asks for minutes.

questions.prompt: How many minutes of approving is that per day?
hints: Count the approvals that still need a person.
Of 1,000 requests, 1,000 − 940 = 60 need approval.
Multiply the approvals by the seconds each takes, then convert seconds to minutes.
questions.onCorrect: Letting low-risk actions run, with a log, leaves people the few decisions that matter.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60 approvals at 5 seconds each are 300 seconds, and 300 ÷ 60 = 5 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the load if every one of the 1,000 requests needed approval. Only 60 do.
That is the time in seconds. The question asks for minutes.

questions.prompt: What is the most, in dollars, that can leave in a day without approval?
hints: The worst case has every refund at the cap.
The cap is $20 and the rate limit is 50 refunds.
Multiply the two.
questions.onCorrect: Limits turn an open-ended risk into a number that a team can decide is acceptable.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 refunds at no more than $20 each give at most 50 × 20 = $1,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two limits. The most that can leave is the product of the cap and the number of refunds.
That is the cap on one refund. The rate limit allows 50 of them.

questions.prompt: What is the most, in dollars, that can leave in a day without approval?
hints: The worst case has every refund at the cap.
The cap is $15 and the rate limit is 30 refunds.
Multiply the two.
questions.onCorrect: Tightening either limit lowers the worst case in proportion, which gives a team a dial to turn.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 refunds at no more than $15 each give at most 30 × 15 = $450.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two limits. Multiply the cap by the number of refunds.
That is the cap on one refund. The rate limit allows 30 of them.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this design, and what is the fix?
hints: Compare what the agent needs with what the borrowed credentials allow.
A prompt cannot withdraw access that the credentials grant.
questions.onCorrect: An agent that borrows full credentials can do whatever the user can, so its identity should be scoped to the task.

acceptedIdeas: It gives the agent more access than its task needs, so give it its own identity with only the scopes the task requires
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It gives the agent more access than its task needs, so give it its own identity with only the scopes the task requires

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, because the employee has approved the agent
It gives the agent more access than its task needs, so give it its own identity with only the scopes the task requires
It is too slow, so cache the credentials
It works only if the system prompt forbids deleting accounts

misconceptions.feedback: The employee's approval does not narrow the credentials, and the agent can still reach everything they can.
Speed is not the problem, and caching credentials would widen their reach in time.
A prompt is only text, and it cannot withdraw access that the credentials grant. The server has to enforce the limit.

questions.prompt: An agent makes 1,200 actions a day, each needing an approval that takes a person 4 seconds. How many minutes of approving is that per day?
hints: Find the total number of seconds first.
1,200 approvals at 4 seconds each.
Divide the seconds by 60.
questions.onCorrect: That is more than an hour and a quarter of approving a day, which is why approval is reserved for risky actions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total in seconds. The question asks for minutes.
That is 1,200 ÷ 60, which leaves out the 4 seconds each.

questions.prompt: Refunds that run without approval are capped at $15 each, and the rate limit is 60 a day. What is the most, in dollars, that can leave in a day without approval?
hints: The worst case has every refund at the cap.
Multiply the rate limit by the cap.
questions.onCorrect: A rate limit and a cap together bound the worst case, whatever the model does.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At most 60 refunds of $15 each, so 60 × 15 = $900.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two limits. The worst case is their product.
That is the cap on one refund. The rate limit allows 60 of them.

questions.prompt: What is the principle of giving an agent only the access its task needs called?
hints: It applies to the identity the agent uses as well as to its tools.
The name says how much access, and of which kind.
questions.onCorrect: With least privilege the reach of any mistake or attack is limited to what the task required.

misconceptions.feedback: An approval gate asks a person to decide before a risky action. The principle of limiting access has another name.
An audit log records what happened. The principle of limiting access has another name.

questions.prompt: What do we call text an agent reads that an attacker could have written, such as a web page?
hints: The word describes how far the agent can rely on the text.
A web page, an email from a stranger and a retrieved document all belong to it.
questions.onCorrect: Any text an attacker could have written is untrusted, however it reached the agent, and may contain instructions.

misconceptions.feedback: Trusted text is what the team wrote. A page that anyone could edit is the opposite.
A permission says what an agent may do. The page is something the agent reads.

questions.prompt: How many of the three capabilities does this agent have?
hints: Take the capabilities one at a time.
Private data: yes. Untrusted content: yes, strangers write emails. Outbound channel: no.
Count the yes answers.
questions.onCorrect: The agent has two capabilities, and the missing third is what stops private data from leaving.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inbox is private data and accepts text from outsiders, which makes it untrusted content too, and the agent has no outbound channel, so it has 2 of the 3.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no tool that sends anything outside, so the third capability is absent.
The inbox gives two: it is private, and outsiders can write into it.

questions.prompt: On average, how many of the 200 attempts get past the filter?
hints: Find the share that the filter misses.
The filter catches 95%, so it misses 5%.
Take 5% of 200.
questions.onCorrect: Even a filter that catches nearly every attempt leaves some through, and a patient attacker needs only one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The filter misses 5% of attempts, and 5% of 200 is 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number the filter catches. The question asks how many get through.
That is the percentage that gets through, and the question asks for the number of attempts out of 200.

questions.prompt: Which change most directly removes a capability for an agent that reads email and can send email?
hints: Look for the change that takes away a capability, not one that asks the model to behave.
Which of the three capabilities can be taken away without stopping the agent's useful work?
questions.onCorrect: Removing the outbound channel breaks the trifecta whatever the model is persuaded to do, which no change to the prompt can guarantee.

acceptedIdeas: Remove the ability to send to external addresses
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Remove the ability to send to external addresses

choices.label: Add a stronger system prompt
Remove the ability to send to external addresses
Raise the temperature
Add more examples to the prompt

misconceptions.feedback: A stronger prompt asks the model to resist, and the attack works by getting text past the model's resistance. All three capabilities remain.
Temperature changes how varied the output is. It does not take away a capability.
Examples change what the model is likely to write. They leave all three capabilities in place.

questions.prompt: How many of the three capabilities does the browser agent have?
hints: The session gives one capability, the pages another, and the links and forms a third.
All three answers in the lines above were yes.
Count the yes answers.
questions.onCorrect: With all three present, the agent is open to the attack, so the design has to remove or contain one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The session gives private data, the pages give untrusted content, and links and forms give an outbound channel, so all 3.

misconceptions.feedback: Following links and submitting forms are outbound requests, so the third capability is present.
The session, the pages and the outbound requests are all present.

questions.prompt: How many of the three capabilities does the summariser have?
hints: Count the yes answers above.
Private data: yes. Untrusted content: no. Outbound: yes.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: A missing untrusted-content leg means no outsider can steer the agent, so the dangerous combination does not form while that holds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It has private data and an outbound channel but no untrusted content, so 2 of the 3.

misconceptions.feedback: The documents are signed and written by the company, so the untrusted-content capability is absent.
Private data and the email tool are both present.

questions.prompt: What is the chance that at least one of the 100 attempts gets through? Give it as a decimal to two places.
hints: It is easier to find the chance that all 100 are caught, and subtract it from 1.
The chance that one attempt is caught is 0.99, so all 100 are caught with probability 0.99 to the power 100.
Subtract that from 1 and round to two places.
questions.onCorrect: A defence that is right nearly every time still loses to an attacker who can try again, because the attacker needs only one success.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chance that all 100 are caught is 0.99¹⁰⁰, about 0.366, so the chance that at least one gets through is 1 − 0.366 = about 0.634, which is 0.63 to two places.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that one attempt is caught. The question asks about at least one of 100 getting through.
That is the chance that every attempt is caught. The question asks for the chance that at least one gets through.
The chance is high but not certain: 100 attempts against a 99% filter leaves a real chance that all are caught.

questions.prompt: Is human approval of outbound email enough to make this design safe?
hints: Think about what a person actually notices in a long message.
An approval is a layer, and the question is whether it can be the only one.
questions.onCorrect: Approval helps, and it fails when the approver does not notice the hidden detail, so it should sit beside a limit enforced in code.

acceptedIdeas: No, because a hurried approver can miss the hidden address, so the recipients should also be restricted in code
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because a hurried approver can miss the hidden address, so the recipients should also be restricted in code

choices.label: Yes, because a person sees every email
Yes, because the agent cannot send without approval
No, because a hurried approver can miss the hidden address, so the recipients should also be restricted in code
No, because approval is never useful

misconceptions.feedback: A person sees the message, but may not see one extra address among many, which is all the attack needs.
The gate does stop unapproved sending, but the attack works through the approved message itself.
Approval is useful as an additional layer. The point is that it is not the only control to rely on.

questions.prompt: An agent reads the user's inbox and fetches any web address that it chooses, with no other tools. How many of the three capabilities does it have?
hints: The inbox gives two capabilities.
A tool that fetches any address can carry data out in the address.
Count the capabilities.
questions.onCorrect: A fetcher that can reach any address counts as an outbound channel, even though nothing is called sending.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inbox is private data and accepts outside text, and fetching any address is an outbound channel because the address can carry data, so it has all 3.

misconceptions.feedback: Fetching any address can carry data to an attacker's server, so the third capability is present.
The inbox gives two capabilities, since it is private and outsiders can write into it.

questions.prompt: A filter catches 98% of injection attempts, and attackers make 500 attempts. On average, how many get past the filter?
hints: Find the share that the filter misses.
The filter catches 98%, so it misses 2%.
Take 2% of 500.
questions.onCorrect: Even a very good filter lets a few attempts through when the attacker can try many times.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The filter misses 2%, and 2% of 500 is 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number the filter catches. The question asks how many get through.
That is the percentage that gets through, not the number of attempts out of 500.

questions.prompt: What name did Simon Willison give to the combination of private data, untrusted content and external communication in one agent?
hints: It has three parts, and the word for the combination suggests how serious it is.
The name has two words, one for how dangerous it is and one for the number of parts.
questions.onCorrect: An agent with all three capabilities can be steered by an attacker to gather private data and send it out.

misconceptions.feedback: Prompt injection is the attack. The combination of capabilities that makes it dangerous has its own name.
Privilege separation is a control. The combination of capabilities has its own name.

questions.prompt: The spans take 1.2 s, 0.8 s, 1.6 s and 1.9 s, one after another. How many seconds did the whole run take?
hints: The four spans run one after another.
The run lasts as long as the four spans put together.
questions.onCorrect: Spans that run in sequence add up to the length of the run that contains them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The spans do not overlap, so the run lasts 1.2 + 0.8 + 1.6 + 1.9 = 5.5 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the longest span only. The four spans run one after another, so their times add.
That leaves out one of the four spans.

questions.prompt: What is the mean latency, in seconds?
hints: Find the total time of the ten runs.
Nine runs of 2 seconds and one of 20 seconds.
Divide the total by 10.
questions.onCorrect: A mean blends the fast and the slow runs into a value that matches neither, so a few slow runs can hide in it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 9 × 2 + 20 = 38 seconds, and 38 ÷ 10 = 3.8 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time of the typical run. The mean includes the slow run as well.
That is the slowest run. The mean averages all ten.

questions.prompt: What is the nearest-rank p95 of these twenty latencies, in seconds?
hints: Find the position first: round 0.95 × n up to a whole number.
0.95 × 20 = 19, so take the 19th value.
Count along the sorted list to the 19th value.
questions.onCorrect: The nearest-rank p95 is an actual observed value, here the second slowest of the twenty runs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The position is ⌈0.95 × 20⌉ = 19, and the 19th smallest value is 4.8 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 20th value, the maximum. The p95 is at position 19.
That is the 18th value. The position is ⌈0.95 × 20⌉ = 19.
That is the mean of the twenty values. The p95 is a position in the sorted list.

questions.prompt: What is the p95 of the eight latencies, in seconds?
hints: The position was 8.
Take the 8th value of the sorted list.
The list ends with 6.0.
questions.onCorrect: With only eight runs the p95 is the maximum, which is why percentiles need enough runs to say anything about a tail.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The position is 8, the last of the eight values, which is 6.0 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the median, p50. The p95 is at position 8.
That is the 7th value. The position for the p95 is 8.

questions.prompt: What is the cost per success, in dollars?
hints: Divide the total spend by the number of successful runs, not by the number of runs.
The total is $27 and there are 90 successes.
questions.onCorrect: The failed runs are paid for but deliver nothing, so their cost is carried by the runs that succeed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: $27 ÷ 90 successes = $0.30 per success.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost per run, $27 ÷ 150. The question asks for the cost per success.
That is the number of failed runs, 150 − 90. The question asks for a cost in dollars.

questions.prompt: What is the new cost per success, in dollars?
hints: Divide the spend by the number of successes.
The spend is $27 and the successes are 135.
questions.onCorrect: The cost per run stayed at $0.18, and the cost per success fell from $0.30 to $0.20 because more runs delivered.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: $27 ÷ 135 = $0.20 per success.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost per run, which did not change. The cost per success divides by the successes.
That is the cost per success before the improvement. Divide by the new number of successes.

questions.prompt: Before storing a trace, what should the team do?
hints: Ask what a team needs from a trace in order to debug and to measure.
Look for the answer that keeps the measurements and drops the sensitive content.
questions.onCorrect: Redaction keeps the structure, timings and counts that debugging and measurement use, and it keeps sensitive content out of the store.

acceptedIdeas: Redact personal data and secrets, and set a retention period
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Redact personal data and secrets, and set a retention period

choices.label: Keep the raw text, because debugging needs everything
Redact personal data and secrets, and set a retention period
Delete every span, because traces are unsafe
Share the traces publicly so that others can help debug

misconceptions.feedback: Debugging rarely needs the raw personal data, and a store of raw emails and tokens is itself a risk.
Without spans there is nothing to measure or debug, so the team would be blind.
Traces hold personal data and secrets, so sharing them publicly would expose both.

questions.prompt: Twenty runs have these sorted latencies in seconds: 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.5, 1.6, 1.8, 1.9, 2.2, 2.5, 3.1, 3.8, 6.2, 11.0. What is the nearest-rank p95, in seconds?
hints: Find the position by rounding 0.95 × 20 up.
The position is 19.
Count along the sorted list to the 19th value.
questions.onCorrect: The p95 is the 19th of twenty values, and here it is well below the maximum of 11.0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The position is ⌈0.95 × 20⌉ = 19, and the 19th value is 6.2 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 20th value, the maximum. The p95 is at position 19.
That is the 18th value. The position is ⌈0.95 × 20⌉ = 19.

questions.prompt: 300 runs cost $45 in total, and 180 of them succeed. What is the cost per success, in dollars?
hints: Divide the total spend by the number of successes.
The total is $45 and there are 180 successes.
questions.onCorrect: Cost per success carries the cost of the failed runs, so it is higher than the cost per run, which is $0.15 here.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: $45 ÷ 180 = $0.25 per success.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost per run, $45 ÷ 300. The question asks for the cost per success.
That is the number of failed runs, 300 − 180. The question asks for a cost in dollars.

questions.prompt: What is the record of one agent run as a tree of spans called?
hints: Each model call and tool call in the run is a span inside it.
The name is also used for a record of the path something took.
questions.onCorrect: A trace lets a team see where a run's time and tokens went, one span at a time.

misconceptions.feedback: A span is one piece of the record, such as a single model call. The whole tree has another name.
A log is a list of events. The tree of nested spans for one run has another name.

questions.prompt: The final answer is right, but the agent deleted a record it should not touch. How is the run graded?
hints: Ask whether the trajectory check was satisfied.
Taking a forbidden action counts against the run, whatever the answer was.
questions.onCorrect: A run that takes a forbidden action is rejected, however correct its final answer is.

choices.label: Pass
Fail
Partial credit, always
It cannot be graded

misconceptions.feedback: The final answer is right, but the forbidden action breaks the trajectory check, so the run cannot be accepted.
Partial credit would reward a run that damaged something, and a forbidden action rules a run out.
The trace records the deletion, so the run can be graded against the rule.

questions.prompt: How many of the six runs pass?
hints: A run needs a correct outcome, no forbidden action, and at most 13 steps.
Runs C and F have wrong outcomes, and run B has a forbidden action.
Count the runs left.
questions.onCorrect: Each check removes some runs, and relaxing one check lets back only the runs that failed it alone.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A, D and E have correct outcomes, no forbidden action and at most 13 steps. B has a forbidden action, and C and F have wrong outcomes, so 3 runs pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count under the 8-step rule. With 13 steps allowed, run D passes as well.
That counts run B, which has a forbidden action and so still fails.
Runs C and F have the wrong outcome, and run B took a forbidden action.

questions.prompt: On average, on how many of the 30 days does the agent fail?
hints: Find the chance of failing on one day.
It succeeds on 90% of days, so it fails on 10%.
Take 10% of 30.
questions.onCorrect: A small failure rate per trial becomes a regular failure over many trials.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The agent fails on 10% of days, and 10% of 30 days is 3 days.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average number of successful days. The question asks about failures.
That is the chance of failing on one day. The question asks about 30 days.

questions.prompt: What is pass^3, the chance that all three trials succeed?
hints: All three must succeed, and the trials are independent.
Multiply the chance of success by itself three times.
questions.onCorrect: Pass^k multiplies the per-trial chance k times, so it falls with every added trial.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All three must succeed, so the chance is 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.512.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one trial. All three must succeed.
That is the chance that at least one succeeds, which is pass@3. The question asks for all three.
That multiplies two trials. There are three.

questions.prompt: What is pass@3, the chance that at least one of the three trials succeeds?
hints: It is easier to find the chance that every trial fails.
Each trial fails with probability 0.2, so all three fail with 0.2 to the power 3.
Subtract that from 1.
questions.onCorrect: At least one success is the opposite of every trial failing, which is why pass@k is found from the failure chance.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chance that all three fail is 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.008, so the chance that at least one succeeds is 1 − 0.008 = 0.992.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one trial. The question asks about at least one of three.
That is the chance that all three succeed, which is pass^3. The question asks for at least one.
That is the chance that all three fail. The question asks for the chance that at least one succeeds.

questions.prompt: What is pass^4, to two decimal places?
hints: Multiply 0.6 by itself four times.
0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36, then multiply by 0.6 again.
Round the result to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: Four trials at 60% give a chance of only about 13% that all succeed, though at least one succeeds nearly every time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.6⁴ = 0.1296, which is 0.13 to two decimal places.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one trial. All four must succeed.
That is pass@4, the chance that at least one succeeds. The question asks about all four.

questions.prompt: What is pass@3?
hints: Subtract the chance that all three fail from 1.
The chance that all fail is 0.027.
questions.onCorrect: Three trials at 70% give a 97.3% chance that at least one succeeds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that all three fail. Subtract it from 1.
That is pass^3, the chance that all three succeed.

questions.prompt: What is the chance of no failure at all in 30 days? Give it as a decimal to two places.
hints: All 30 days must succeed, and the days are independent.
The chance is 0.9 raised to the power 30.
Use a calculator and round to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: Reliability falls off quickly as trials accumulate, so a flawless run of 30 needs a per-trial success rate much higher than 90%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All 30 days must succeed, so the chance is 0.9³⁰, which is about 0.0424, or 0.04 to two places.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one day. Thirty must all succeed.
That is the chance of at least one failure, 1 − 0.04. The question asks for no failure.

questions.prompt: How much does one run of the gate cost, in dollars?
hints: Count the runs first.
30 tasks with 5 trials each.
Multiply the number of runs by the cost of one.
questions.onCorrect: The gate's cost is the number of tasks times the trials times the cost per run, which is why the suite should be small and well chosen.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 tasks × 5 trials = 150 runs, and 150 × $0.12 = $18.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of runs. Multiply by the cost of one run.
That is 5 × $0.12, the cost of the trials for one task. There are 30 tasks.

questions.prompt: Which measure should the team report for this agent?
hints: Ask whether one success is enough or whether every trial matters.
No one is available to retry the task.
questions.onCorrect: When every trial must succeed, pass^k is the measure that answers the question, and it falls with k.

acceptedIdeas: pass^k, because every trial has to succeed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pass^k, because every trial has to succeed

choices.label: pass@k, because one success in k trials is enough
The final answer of the best trial
pass^k, because every trial has to succeed
The mean latency

misconceptions.feedback: Pass@k measures the chance of at least one success, which is the right question only when a retry is cheap.
Reporting the best trial hides the failures that a customer would have met.
Latency measures speed, not whether the task is done correctly.

questions.prompt: Each trial of a task succeeds with probability 0.9, independently. What is pass^4, to two decimal places?
hints: All four trials must succeed.
Multiply 0.9 by itself four times.
Round the result to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: Four trials at 90% give a chance of only about two in three that all succeed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.9⁴ = 0.6561, which is 0.66 to two decimal places.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one trial. All four must succeed.
The chance of four successes in a row is below 1, since each trial can fail.

questions.prompt: Each trial of a task succeeds with probability 0.7, independently. What is pass@2, the chance that at least one of two trials succeeds?
hints: Find the chance that both trials fail.
Each trial fails with probability 0.3.
Subtract the chance that both fail from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Pass@k is one minus the chance that every trial fails, so it rises with k.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both fail with probability 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09, so at least one succeeds with probability 1 − 0.09 = 0.91.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that both trials succeed, which is pass^2. The question asks for at least one.
That is the chance that both fail. Subtract it from 1.

questions.prompt: What is the sequence of actions an agent took in a run, as opposed to its final answer, called?
hints: It is what a trace of the run records, step by step.
It can be graded for forbidden actions and for the number of steps.
questions.onCorrect: Grading the trajectory catches runs that reach a right answer by a path that should not have been taken.

misconceptions.feedback: The outcome is the state the run leaves. The sequence of actions that led to it has another name.
A trace is the recorded tree of spans. The sequence of actions it records has another name.

questions.prompt: How many actions is a 2% sample of 1,500 actions?
hints: Convert the percentage to a fraction of the actions.
2% is 0.02, and the day has 1,500 actions.
Multiply 1,500 by 0.02.
questions.onCorrect: A sample of a few percent of a large number of actions is small enough for a person to read closely.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 20% of 1,500. The sample is 2%.
That is 5% of 1,500. The sample is 2%.

questions.prompt: What is the agreement rate, as a percentage?
hints: Divide the number of matches by the number of proposals.
372 matches out of 400 proposals.
Multiply the result by 100 to get a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: An agreement rate compares the agent's proposals with decisions a person made, which gives evidence without any action being taken.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of disagreements, 400 − 372. The question asks for the agreement rate as a percentage.
That is the agreement as a fraction. The question asks for a percentage.

questions.prompt: Which stage runs the agent without executing its actions?
hints: Ask in which stage the proposals are carried out, whether by the agent or by a person.
In one stage nothing the agent proposes is run, and a person only compares afterwards.
questions.onCorrect: In shadow mode the proposals are recorded and compared with human decisions, and no action is carried out.

choices.label: Act
Assist
Shadow
Retire

misconceptions.feedback: In act mode the agent executes within its permissions, so its actions do take effect.
In assist mode a person accepts or rejects each proposal, and the accepted ones are carried out.
Retire is not a stage of the rollout, and it would mean withdrawing the agent.

questions.prompt: What is the sampled error rate, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Divide the number of wrong actions by the size of the sample.
2 wrong out of 30 sampled.
Multiply the result by 100 to get a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: An error rate from a small sample is noisy, so the trigger asks for a look at the cause and not for a verdict.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 ÷ 30 is about 0.0667, which is 6.7%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 30 ÷ 2, the sample per error. The error rate is the errors divided by the sample.
That is the number of wrong actions. The question asks for a percentage of the 30 sampled.

questions.prompt: Which NIST AI RMF function covers policies, roles and accountability?
hints: Its name is the verb for exercising authority over something.
The other three functions are Map, Measure and Manage.
questions.onCorrect: Govern sets up the policies and accountability that the other functions rely on.

misconceptions.feedback: Manage prioritises and acts on risks. The function for policies and roles has another name.
Map establishes context and identifies risks. The function for policies and roles has another name.
Measure analyses and tracks risks. The function for policies and roles has another name.

questions.prompt: How many actions does a person look at in a day?
hints: Add the reads sampled, the small writes sampled and the costly writes approved.
The counts are 12, 10 and 50.
questions.onCorrect: Tiering concentrates the human effort on the few risky actions, so 72 looks cover a day of 1,500 actions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of actions the agent makes. A person looks at only the sampled and approved ones.
That adds the sampled reads and small writes and leaves out the costly writes, which are all approved.

questions.prompt: How many actions does a person look at in a day?
hints: Add the counts from the lines above.
The counts are 16, 9 and 20.
questions.onCorrect: A different mix of actions changes the load, which is why the tiers and the sampling rates are chosen together.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of actions the agent makes. A person looks at only the sampled and approved ones.
That leaves out the 20 costly writes, which are all approved.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with this design?
hints: Think about what a person can notice in a few seconds per action.
Ask where the approval would do the most good.
questions.onCorrect: A person who approves at speed checks nothing, so approval should be reserved for risky actions and the rest sampled.

acceptedIdeas: Approving at that speed becomes a reflex, so it delays the work without checking it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Approving at that speed becomes a reflex, so it delays the work without checking it

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, because a person sees every action
Approving at that speed becomes a reflex, so it delays the work without checking it
Approval is never useful, so the agent should act alone
The agent will run out of tokens if a person approves

misconceptions.feedback: Seeing an action for a few seconds is not the same as checking it, and the volume makes the review a reflex.
Approval is valuable for the riskiest actions. The design's fault is applying it to all of them.
Approval does not use tokens. The trouble is the volume of work for the approvers.

questions.prompt: A team reviews 3% of the 2,000 actions an agent makes in a day. How many actions is that?
hints: Convert the percentage to a fraction.
